front: What are the primary causative species of Brucella and their main animal reservoirs?
back:
• B. melitensis: Goats and sheep (most common and most virulent human pathogen).
• B. abortus: Cattle and cows.
• B. suis: Swine and pigs.
• B. canis: Dogs.

front: What are the main routes of transmission of Brucellosis to humans?
back:
• Ingestion: Consuming raw unpasteurized milk, butter, or soft cheese.
• Occupational Contact: Direct skin/mucous membrane exposure to animal tissues, placenta, or blood
(veterinarians, farmers, butchers).
• Inhalation: Aerosols in laboratory settings or abattoirs.

front: What is the characteristic fever pattern and key systemic clinical features of Brucellosis?
back:
• Fever Pattern: Undulant fever (wave-like fever rising in evening/night and falling by morning).
• Profuse Sweating: Moldy/musty odor, especially at night.
• Constitutional Symptoms: Drenching sweats, rigors, anorexia, weight loss, generalized body aches.
• Physical Signs: Hepatosplenomegaly and generalized lymphadenopathy.

front: What is the most frequent focal musculoskeletal complication of chronic or untreated Brucellosis?
back:
• Osteoarticular Involvement: Affects up to 50% of patients.
• Sacroiliitis: Most common joint complication in young adults.
• Spondylodiscitis: Inflammation of intervertebral discs and adjacent lumbar vertebrae in older adults.
• Peripheral Arthritis: Asymmetric monoarthritis or oligoarthritis (knees, hips).

front: What is the most serious and potentially fatal organ complication of Brucellosis?
back:
• Neurobrucellosis: Meningitis, encephalitis, cranial nerve palsies (CN VIII deafness).
• Brucella Endocarditis: Most dangerous complication; accounts for the majority of brucellosis-related
deaths.
• Affected Valve: Aortic valve is most frequently damaged, requiring valve replacement.

front: What laboratory culture methods are used to diagnose Brucellosis?
back:
• Castaneda Medium: Specialized biphasic culture medium (solid agar + liquid broth in one bottle).
• Incubation Time: Fastidious, slow-growing organism requiring incubation for up to 4 weeks.
• Diagnostic Yield: Bone marrow culture has higher sensitivity (90%) than blood culture (50-70%).

front: How is the Rose Bengal test used in Brucellosis diagnosis?
back:
• Type of Test: Rapid slide agglutination screening test.
• Sensitivity: Highly sensitive for detecting antibodies against Brucella lipopolysaccharide.
• Clinical Utility: Used for fast field screening; positive results must be confirmed by quantitative tube
agglutination (SAT).

front: What antibody titers on the Standard Tube Agglutination Test (SAT) confirm active Brucellosis?
back:
• Significant Titer: SAT titer >= 1:160 in non-endemic areas (>= 1:320 in endemic areas).
• Antibody Detected: Early acute phase is dominated by IgM antibodies.
• Fourfold Rise: Paired sera showing a 4-fold increase in titer 2 weeks apart is diagnostic.

front: What is the role of 2-Mercaptoethanol (2-ME) test in Brucellosis serology?
back:
• Mechanism: 2-ME destroys IgM disulfide bonds, leaving only IgG intact.
• Clinical Significance: Differentiates active chronic/relapsing infection (IgG present) from early acute
infection or past immunity.
• Titer Threshold: 2-ME SAT titer >= 1:80 indicates active ongoing infection.

front: What is the first-line oral antibiotic combination for uncomplicated adult Brucellosis?
back:
• Standard WHO Regimen: Doxycycline (100 mg BID) + Rifampicin (600-900 mg daily).
• Duration: Minimum of 6 weeks continuously.
• Alternative Regimen: Doxycycline (6 weeks) + Intramuscular Streptomycin (15 days) — lower relapse
rate.

front: What treatment regimen is indicated for Brucellosis in children under 8 years of age?
back:
• Contraindication: Tetracyclines/Doxycycline are avoided due to dental staining and bone growth delay.
• First-Line Child Regimen: Rifampicin + Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).


• Treatment Duration: 6 weeks.

front: What treatment regimen is safe for pregnant women with Brucellosis?
back:
• Avoided Drugs: Doxycycline (teratogenic/bone toxicity) and Aminoglycosides (ototoxicity).
• Safe Regimen: Rifampicin alone or combined with TMP-SMX (until 36 weeks gestation).
• Duration: 6 weeks.

front: What antibiotic regimen is required for Neurobrucellosis or Brucella Endocarditis?
back:
• Triple Drug Therapy: Doxycycline + Rifampicin + Ceftriaxone (or Cotrimoxazole).
• Extended Duration: 3 to 6 months.
• Surgical Indication: Urgent valve replacement is often necessary in endocarditis.

front: What histological lesion is characteristic of Brucella infection in tissues?
back:
• Granuloma Type: Non-caseating epithelioid granulomas.
• Location: Reticuloendothelial system (bone marrow, liver, spleen, lymph nodes).
• Cellular Response: Facultative intracellular pathogen inside macrophages.

front: What is Faget's sign in Brucellosis?
back:
• Definition: Relative bradycardia (pulse rate is unexpectedly slow relative to high fever).
• Clinical Association: Seen in Brucellosis, Typhoid fever, Yellow fever, and Legionnaires' disease.

front: How can human Brucellosis be prevented effectively?
back:
• Milk Hygiene: Pasteurization or boiling of all milk and dairy products.
• Occupational Safety: Protective gloves, aprons, and masks for slaughterhouse workers and veterinarians.
• Animal Control: Vaccination of livestock (Rev-1 for sheep/goats, Strain 19/RB51 for cattle). *No human
vaccine exists.*
🐀 Typhoid Fever

front: What is the causative organism of Typhoid fever and its main reservoir?
back:
• Causative Agent: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (and S. Paratyphi A, B, C).
• Microbiology: Gram-negative, motile, flagellated non-spore-forming bacillus.
• Reservoir: Humans are the ONLY natural reservoir.

front: What are the primary antigens of Salmonella typhi?
back:
• O Antigen: Somatic endotoxic lipopolysaccharide outer membrane antigen.
• H Antigen: Protein flagellar antigen responsible for motility.
• Vi Antigen: Virulence surface capsular polysaccharide that prevents phagocytosis and complement lysis.

front: What is the timeline of clinical features during Week 1 of untreated Typhoid fever?
back:
• Fever: Step-ladder pattern (rises gradually each day, reaching 40°C).
• Heart Rate: Relative bradycardia (Faget's sign).


• Abdomen: Epistaxis, abdominal pain, constipation (common in early adult stage), dry cough.

front: What are the classic clinical features during Week 2 of untreated Typhoid fever?
back:
• Rose Spots: Transient, pink, blanching macules on upper chest/abdomen (days 7-10).
• Abdomen: Marked distension, pea-soup diarrhea, splenohepatomegaly.
• Mental State: Typhoid state (apathy, delirium, coma vigil, subsultus tendinum).

front: What are the major life-threatening complications occurring in Week 3 of Typhoid fever?
back:
• Pathology: Hyperplasia and ulceration of Peyer's patches in terminal ileum.
• Intestinal Hemorrhage: Sudden drop in body temperature and blood pressure, melena/bright red blood.
• Bowel Perforation: Sudden acute right lower quadrant peritonitis (highest mortality).

front: What is the diagnostic yield of blood culture in Typhoid fever across different weeks?
back:
• Week 1: Highest sensitivity (80-90% positive bacteremia).
• Week 2: 50% positive.
• Week 3-4: Sensitivity drops significantly.

front: When do stool and urine cultures reach peak diagnostic positivity in Typhoid fever?
back:
• Peak Time: Weeks 2 and 3 of illness.
• Pathophysiology: S. typhi excreted into bile from gallbladder and shed into gut feces and urinary tract.

front: What specimen provides the highest overall diagnostic sensitivity for S. typhi at any stage?
back: • Bone Marrow Culture: Sensitivity > 90% even after starting antimicrobial therapy.

front: How is the Widal serological test interpreted in Typhoid fever?
back:
• O Titer >= 1:160: Indicates recent active acute infection.
• H Titer >= 1:160: Indicates past infection or vaccination.
• Diagnostic Rule: A 4-fold rise in O antibody titer between acute and convalescent sera is required.

front: What Complete Blood Count (CBC) changes are classic for uncomplicated Typhoid fever?
back:
• WBC Count: Leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis.
• Eosinophils: Aneosinophilia (complete absence of eosinophils).
• Complications: Leukocytosis indicates intestinal perforation or pyogenic superinfection.

front: Where does S. typhi persist in chronic typhoid carriers, and how is it defined?
back:
• Anatomic Reservoir: Gallbladder mucosa and gallstones.
• Definition: Excretion of S. typhi in stool or urine for > 1 year after acute illness.
• Risk Factor: Pre-existing cholelithiasis (gallstones).

front: What is the medical treatment of choice for chronic Typhoid carriers?
back:
• First-Line Oral Drug: Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin for 4 to 6 weeks.
• Alternative: High-dose Amoxicillin + Probenecid for 6 weeks.
• Surgical Option: Cholecystectomy if gallstones are present and antibiotics fail.

front: What is the preferred empiric antibiotic treatment for severe or complicated Typhoid fever?
back:
• First-Line IV: Ceftriaxone (2g IV daily) or Azithromycin (oral).
• Quinolone Resistance: Fluoroquinolones (Ciprofloxacin) have high resistance rates in South Asia/Egypt.
• Duration: 10 to 14 days.

front: What drug is added to antibiotics in severe Typhoid fever with delirium or shock?
back: • High-Dose Dexamethasone: Reduces mortality in severe typhoid with shock or altered sensorium.

front: What are the available typhoid vaccines and their administration?
back:
• Ty21a: Live attenuated oral vaccine (3-4 doses every other day; for ages >= 6 years).
• Vi Capsular Polysaccharide: Injectable IM vaccine (single dose; for ages >= 2 years).
• Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (TCV): Injectable (single dose; approved for infants >= 6 months).

front: What is the mechanism of bowel perforation in Typhoid fever?
back:
• Location: Terminal ileum (within 50 cm of ileocecal valve).
• Pathology: Necrosis of Peyer's patches leads to longitudinal ulcers along the long axis of intestine.
• Management: Urgent surgical repair/resection + broad-spectrum IV coverage.

front: What is the difference between S. typhi longitudinal ulcers and TB transverse gut ulcers?
back:
• Typhoid Ulcers: Longitudinal along the long axis of the ileum (over Peyer's patches).
• TB Ulcers: Transverse (circumferential) along the lymphatics, leading to strictures.

front: How is a cholagogue used in identifying chronic Typhoid carriers?
back:
• Mechanism: Administration of a saline purge or fat meal stimulates gallbladder contraction.
• Diagnostic Value: Evacuates bile-rich stool, greatly enhancing S. typhi isolation yield.
🐀 Meningitis

front: What are the most common bacterial pathogens causing acute meningitis by age group?
back:
• Neonate (< 1 month): Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes.
• Infants & Children (1 month - 18 yrs): Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Hib.
• Adults (19 - 50 yrs): S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis.
• Elderly (> 50 yrs / Immunocompromised): S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes.

front: What is the classic triad of acute bacterial meningitis?
back:
• Classic Triad: Fever, Nuchal Rigidity (stiff neck), Altered Mental Status.
• Associated Signs: Severe headache, photophobia, vomiting, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign.

front: How are Kernig's and Brudzinski's meningeal signs elicited?
back:
• Kernig's Sign: Flex hip to 90°, passive extension of knee causes severe pain/resistance.
• Brudzinski's Sign: Passive flexion of neck causes involuntary flexion of hips and knees.

front: What physical exam finding is specific for Meningococcal Meningitis (N. meningitidis)?
back:
• Petechial / Purpuric Rash: Non-blanching skin rash on trunk and lower extremities.
• Complication: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (hemorrhagic adrenal necrosis, DIC, fulminant shock).

front: What are the normal CSF parameters in healthy adults?
back:
• Opening Pressure: 10 - 20 cm H2O.
• WBC Count: < 5 cells/μL (all lymphocytes).
• Protein: 15 - 45 mg/dL.
• Glucose: 50 - 80 mg/dL (or >= 60% of simultaneous blood glucose).

front: What is the CSF profile in Acute Bacterial Meningitis?
back:
• Opening Pressure: Elevated (> 20-30 cm H2O).


• WBC Count: 1,000 - 10,000+ cells/μL (marked Neutrophils / PMNs predominance > 80%).
• Protein: Markedly elevated (> 100-500 mg/dL).
• Glucose: Markedly decreased (< 40 mg/dL or CSF/blood glucose ratio < 0.4).

front: What is the CSF profile in Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis?
back:
• Opening Pressure: Normal or slightly elevated.
• WBC Count: 10 - 500 cells/μL (predominantly Lymphocytes).
• Protein: Normal or slightly elevated (50-100 mg/dL).
• Glucose: NORMAL (> 60% of blood glucose).

front: What is the CSF profile in Tuberculous (TB) or Fungal Meningitis?
back:
• Opening Pressure: Markedly elevated.
• WBC Count: 100 - 500 cells/μL (Lymphocytes predominance).
• Protein: Extremely elevated (100 - 1000+ mg/dL).
• Glucose: Markedly low (< 30 mg/dL).

front: When is a CT scan of the brain required BEFORE performing Lumbar Puncture?
back:
• Indications: Focal neurological deficits, new onset seizures, papilledema, severely altered consciousness
(GCS < 10), immunocompromised state.
• Purpose: Rule out mass lesion/herniation risk.

front: What is the empiric antibiotic treatment for acute bacterial meningitis in adults (19-50 yrs)?
back:
• Regimen: Ceftriaxone (2g IV q12h) + Vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h).
• Coverage: Ceftriaxone covers N. meningitidis; Vancomycin covers penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae.

front: Why and when is Ampicillin added to empiric meningitis therapy?
back:
• Added In: Neonates (< 1 mo) and Adults > 50 yrs or immunocompromised.
• Target Pathogen: Listeria monocytogenes (inherently resistant to cephalosporins).

front: What is the role and timing of Dexamethasone in acute bacterial meningitis?
back:
• Indication: Reduces neurological sequelae (deafness) in S. pneumoniae and Hib meningitis.
• Timing: Administered 15-20 minutes BEFORE or WITH the first dose of IV antibiotics.
• Dose: 10 mg IV q6h for 4 days.

front: What is the chemoprophylaxis regimen for close contacts of Meningococcal Meningitis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: Rifampicin (600 mg BID for 2 days).
• Alternatives: Single dose Ciprofloxacin (500 mg PO) or single dose Ceftriaxone (250 mg IM).

front: What is the chemoprophylaxis recommendation for Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib)?
back:
• Indication: All household contacts if there is an unvaccinated child < 4 years old.
• Drug: Oral Rifampicin (600 mg once daily for 4 days).

front: What are the characteristic Gram stain findings for the major meningitis bacteria?
back:
• Neisseria meningitidis: Gram-negative kidney bean-shaped diplococci (intracellular).
• Streptococcus pneumoniae: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci.
• Listeria monocytogenes: Gram-positive rods with tumbling motility.
• Haemophilus influenzae: Small Gram-negative coccobacilli.

front: What CSF cobweb clot (pellicle) formation indicates?
back:
• Diagnostic Sign: Classical for Tuberculous Meningitis upon standing CSF overnight due to extremely high
fibrinogen/protein levels.

front: Which cranial nerve is most commonly damaged as a neurological complication of meningitis?
back:
• Cranial Nerve VIII (Vestibulocochlear): Sensorineural hearing loss is the most common long-term deficit.
• Other Cranial Nerves: CN VI (abducens palsy due to elevated ICP).

front: What is the primary reservoir and transmission of Listeria monocytogenes?
back:
• Transmission: Ingestion of unpasteurized soft cheeses, cold deli meats, unwashed raw vegetables.
• Characteristics: Psychrophilic (multiplies at refrigeration temperatures 4°C).

front: What is the preferred treatment for confirmed Listeria monocytogenes meningitis?
back:
• Drug of Choice: High-dose Ampicillin (2g IV q4h) + Gentamicin.
• Penicillin-Allergic Alternative: Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

front: What meningitis vaccines are routinely administered?
back:
• Meningococcal Vaccines: MenACWY (conjugate) and MenB (recombinant).
• Pneumococcal Vaccines: PCV15/PCV20 (conjugate) and PPSV23.
• Hib Vaccine: Conjugate vaccine given in infancy.

front: What isolation precautions are required for patients with suspected bacterial meningitis?
back:
• Droplet Precautions: Required for Neisseria meningitidis and Hib until 24 hours of effective antibiotic
therapy is completed.

front: What is Mollaret's meningitis?
back:
• Definition: Recurrent benign aseptic meningitis caused by Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 (HSV-2).
🐀 Encephalitis

front: What is the most common cause of sporadic, fatal viral encephalitis worldwide?
back:
• Pathogen: Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1).
• Anatomic Tropism: Temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex.

front: How does clinical presentation of Encephalitis differ from Meningitis?
back:
• Meningitis: Meningeal irritation (stiff neck, photophobia) with intact brain function.
• Encephalitis: Brain parenchymal involvement — altered mental status, confusion, personality changes,
seizures, focal neurological deficits.

front: What olfactory symptom is pathognomonic for temporal lobe HSV-1 Encephalitis?
back: • Olfactory Hallucinations (Aura): Smell of burnt rubber or rotting meat preceding seizures or confusion.

front: What is the non-invasive gold standard diagnostic test for HSV Encephalitis?
back:
• Test: CSF Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) for HSV DNA.
• Sensitivity/Specificity: > 95% sensitive and specific.

front: What electroencephalogram (EEG) pattern is classic for HSV-1 Encephalitis?
back: • EEG Pattern: Periodic Lateralized Epileptiform Discharges (PLEDs) over the temporal lobes.

front: What imaging modality is most sensitive for HSV Encephalitis?
back:
• MRI Brain: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and edematous changes in the medial temporal and inferior frontal
lobes.

front: What is the immediate empiric treatment for suspected viral Encephalitis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: High-dose Intravenous Acyclovir (10 mg/kg IV q8h).
• Urgency: Must be initiated immediately upon clinical suspicion before CSF PCR confirmation to reduce
mortality.

front: What key side effect must be monitored during IV Acyclovir therapy?
back:
• Crystalluria & Acute Kidney Injury: Due to intrarenal precipitation of acyclovir crystals.
• Prevention: Aggressive IV hydration and dose adjustment based on renal function.

front: What arbovirus is a major cause of mosquito-borne encephalitis in North America?
back:
• West Nile Virus (WNV): Transmitted by Culex mosquitoes.
• Key Clinical Feature: Flaccid paralysis (polio-like syndrome) and tremors.

front: What viral cause of encephalitis is transmitted by rabid animal bites?
back:
• Rabies Virus (Lyssavirus): Rhabdovirus causing hydrophobic spasms, agitation, paralysis.


• Histology: Negri bodies in Purkinje cells.

front: What autoimmune encephalitis mimics viral encephalitis and presents with psychiatric symptoms?
back:
• Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis: Seen in young females, associated with ovarian teratomas.
• Clinical Presentation: Psychosis, dyskinesias, autonomic instability.

front: What is Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)?
back:
• Pathology: Progressive fatal neurodegenerative disorder occurring years after primary Measles virus
infection.
🐀 Hepatitis

front: What are the primary modes of transmission for Hepatitis A and E vs B, C, and D?
back:
• Enteric (Fecal-Oral): Hepatitis A (HAV) and Hepatitis E (HEV) — via contaminated food/water.
• Parenteral / Blood-borne / Sexual: Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV), Hepatitis D (HDV).

front: What is the clinical significance of Hepatitis E in pregnant women?
back:
• High Mortality: HEV infection in 3rd trimester of pregnancy has a 20% mortality rate due to fulminant
hepatic failure.

front: What genome structure is unique to Hepatitis B Virus among hepatitis viruses?
back:
• Hepatitis B: Partially double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae).
• All Other Hepatitis Viruses (A, C, D, E): Single-stranded RNA viruses.

front: What does Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) signify in serology?
back: • Significance: Indicates active ongoing infection (either acute or chronic). First marker to appear.

front: What does Anti-HBs antibody signify in Hepatitis B serology?
back:
• Significance: Indicates immunity against HBV (either from recovery after natural infection or successful
vaccination).

front: How do you distinguish HBV immunity from natural infection vs vaccination?
back:
• Immunity from Vaccination: Anti-HBs POSITIVE, Anti-HBc NEGATIVE.
• Immunity from Natural Infection: Anti-HBs POSITIVE, Anti-HBc POSITIVE (IgG).

front: What does Anti-HBc IgM indicate in Hepatitis B serology?
back: • Significance: Indicates acute or recent HBV infection (< 6 months). Sole marker during window period.

front: What is the 'Window Period' in Hepatitis B infection?
back:
• Definition: Interval between clearance of HBsAg and appearance of Anti-HBs.
• Sole Diagnostic Marker: Anti-HBc IgM is the ONLY positive marker.

front: What does HBeAg indicate in Hepatitis B serology?
back: • Significance: Indicates high active viral replication and high infectivity.

front: How is Chronic Hepatitis B defined serologically?
back: • Definition: Persistence of HBsAg for >= 6 months.

front: What is Hepatitis D Virus (HDV) dependency on Hepatitis B?
back: • Requirement: HDV is a defective delta RNA virus that requires HBsAg coat to assemble and infect.

front: What is the difference between HBV/HDV Co-infection vs Superinfection?
back:
• Co-infection: Simultaneous acute HBV and HDV infection (usually resolves, low chronicity).
• Superinfection: Acute HDV in a chronic HBV carrier (high risk of fulminant hepatitis and rapid cirrhosis >
80%).

front: What is the screening test and confirmation test for Hepatitis C (HCV)?
back:
• Screening Test: Anti-HCV IgG antibody ELISA.
• Confirmation Test: HCV RNA PCR (qualitative/quantitative) to confirm active ongoing infection.

front: What percentage of acute Hepatitis C infections progress to Chronic Hepatitis C?
back: • Chronicity Rate: 75% - 85% of acute HCV cases become chronic (highest among hepatitis viruses).

front: What is the modern curative treatment for Chronic Hepatitis C?
back:
• Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs): Sofosbuvir, Velpatasvir, Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir.
• Cure Rate (SVR12): > 95% cure rate with 8 to 12 weeks of oral therapy.

front: What first-line oral antivirals are used for Chronic Hepatitis B?
back: • Nucleos(t)ide Analogues: Entecavir or Tenofovir (TDF / TAF) — high barrier to resistance.

front: What post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is given for non-immune workers exposed to HBsAg+ blood?
back: • PEP Regimen: 1 dose of Hepatitis B Immune Globulin (HBIG) + start HepB vaccine series within 24 hours.

front: What is considered an adequate protective anti-HBs antibody level post-vaccination?
back: • Protective Titer: Anti-HBs >= 10 mIU/mL (>= 100 mIU/mL is optimal in healthcare workers).

front: What percentage of healthy adults fail to respond to standard 3-dose HepB vaccine?
back: • Non-Responders: 10% - 15% of adults.

front: What extrahepatic manifestations are associated with Hepatitis B vs Hepatitis C?
back:
• Hepatitis B: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), Membranous glomerulonephritis.
• Hepatitis C: Mixed Essential Cryoglobulinemia, Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT), Membranoproliferative
GN.

front: Which hepatitis virus carries the highest risk of primary Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)?
back:
• Hepatitis B: Can cause HCC even in the absence of pre-existing cirrhosis (DNA integration into host
genome).
• Hepatitis C: Causes HCC primarily secondary to established cirrhosis.

front: What liver enzyme pattern is characteristic of acute viral hepatitis?
back: • ALT & AST: Markedly elevated (> 1000 U/L), with ALT > AST.

front: What is Councilman body in liver pathology?
back: • Definition: Apoptotic, acidophilic/eosinophilic hepatocyte seen in viral hepatitis.

front: What is the prevention of perinatal HBV transmission from infected mothers to newborns?
back:
• Newborn PEP: Administer HBIG + 1st dose HepB vaccine within 12 hours of birth.
🐀 Cholangitis & Liver Abscess

front: What is Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad in acute cholangitis?
back:
• Charcot's Triad: Fever/Chills, Jaundice, Right Upper Quadrant Pain.
• Reynolds' Pentad: Charcot's triad + Hypotension (Shock) + Altered Mental Status (indicates severe
suppurative cholangitis).

front: What is the definitive initial management for acute ascending cholangitis?
back:
• Management: Biliary decompression via ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) + IV
broad-spectrum antibiotics.

front: What are the two major types of liver abscesses?
back:
• Pyogenic Liver Abscess: Bacterial (E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staph aureus) — usually multiple.
• Amoebic Liver Abscess: Protozoal (Entamoeba histolytica) — usually single in right lobe.

front: What is the characteristic fluid appearance of an Amoebic Liver Abscess aspirate?
back: • Aspirate Appearance: 'Anchovy paste' or chocolate-brown odorless pus.

front: What is the primary treatment of choice for Amoebic Liver Abscess?
back:
• Medical Treatment: Metronidazole (or Tinidazole) for 10 days followed by a luminal agent (Paromomycin
or Diloxanide furoate).
• Surgical Aspiration: Reserved only for very large abscesses (> 5 cm) at risk of rupture.

front: What is the typical route of bacterial entry in Pyogenic Liver Abscess?
back:
• Biliary Tract: Ascending cholangitis secondary to gallstones or stricture (most common).
• Portal Vein: Pylephlebitis from appendicitis or diverticulitis.

front: How do Pyogenic and Amoebic liver abscesses differ on ultrasound?
back:
• Pyogenic: Multiple, complex, septated hypoechoic lesions in both lobes.
• Amoebic: Single, well-demarcated round hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe (subcapsular).

front: What diagnostic serological test confirms Amoebic Liver Abscess?
back: • Amoebic Serology (ELISA): Positive in > 95% of cases (stool microscopy is often negative).

front: What bacterial organism is a leading cause of pyogenic liver abscess in diabetic patients in Asia?
back: • Klebsiella pneumoniae (hypervirulent K1/K2 capsular serotype) — risk of metastatic endophthalmitis.

front: What is Hydatid cyst of the liver?
back:
• Causative Agent: Echinococcus granulosus tapeworm.
• Imaging Finding: Well-defined cyst with internal daughter cysts ('cartwheel' or 'honeycomb' pattern) and
eggshell calcification.

front: What major complication occurs if a Hydatid cyst ruptures during aspiration?
back:
• Anaphylactic Shock: Rupture releases fluid causing severe allergic reaction/anaphylaxis and secondary
peritoneal seeding.

front: What is the PAIR procedure for Hydatid Cyst?
back:
• PAIR: Puncture, Aspiration, Injection of scolicidal agent (hypertonic saline or ethanol), Re-aspiration.
🐀 Pneumonia

front: What is the most common cause of Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)?
back: • Streptococcus pneumoniae (Pneumococcus): Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci.

front: What sputum appearance is characteristic of Pneumococcal vs Klebsiella Pneumonia?
back:
• Streptococcus pneumoniae: Rust-colored sputum.
• Klebsiella pneumoniae: Red currant jelly sputum (thick, bloody).

front: What are the key features of Mycoplasma pneumoniae ('Walking Pneumonia')?
back:
• Population: Young adults, military recruits, college students.
• Extrapulmonary Signs: Erythema multiforme, hemolytic anemia (Cold Agglutinins IgM), bullous
myringitis.

front: What are the clinical hallmarks of Legionella pneumophila pneumonia?
back:
• Source: Contaminated air conditioning systems, water towers, showers.
• Key Signs: High fever, hyponatremia, diarrhea, confusion.
• Diagnosis: Urinary Legionella antigen test.

front: What criteria define the CURB-65 severity score for CAP?
back:
• C: Confusion.
• U: Urea > 7 mmol/L (BUN > 19 mg/dL).
• R: Respiratory Rate >= 30/min.
• B: Blood pressure (SBP < 90 or DBP <= 60 mmHg).
• 65: Age >= 65 years.

front: How does CURB-65 score guide hospital admission for CAP?
back:
• Score 0-1: Outpatient management (low risk).
• Score 2: Inpatient general ward admission.
• Score >= 3: Severe CAP — consider ICU admission.

front: What is the empiric outpatient antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated CAP?
back: • Healthy Adult: Amoxicillin (high dose) or Macrolide (Azithromycin/Clarithromycin) or Doxycycline.

front: What is the empiric inpatient treatment for severe CAP?
back:
• Ward: IV Beta-lactam (Ceftriaxone) + IV Macrolide (Azithromycin) OR Respiratory Fluoroquinolone
(Levofloxacin).
• ICU: Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin + Vancomycin (if MRSA suspected).

front: What defines Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)?
back:
• HAP: Pneumonia developing >= 48 hours after hospital admission.
• VAP: Pneumonia developing >= 48 hours after endotracheal intubation.
• Major Pathogens: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, Acinetobacter.

front: What radiological pattern distinguishes Lobar vs Bronchopneumonia vs Interstitial Pneumonia?
back:
• Lobar: Homogeneous consolidation confined to one lobe (S. pneumoniae).
• Bronchopneumonia: Patchy infiltrates centered around bronchioles (Staph aureus).
• Interstitial: Bilateral reticulonodular/ground-glass infiltrates (Viral / Mycoplasma).

front: What pathogen causes post-influenza secondary bacterial pneumonia with cavitary lesions?
back: • Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA): Causes necrotizing pneumonia with pneumatoceles/cavities.

front: What is Aspiration Pneumonia and its classic anatomical location?
back:
• Risk Factors: Alcoholism, stroke, coma, seizure, poor dental hygiene.
• Location: Right lower lobe (supine: posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe).
• Organisms: Anaerobes + oral flora.

front: What antibiotic is preferred for lung abscess or aspiration pneumonia containing anaerobes?
back: • Drug of Choice: Ampicillin-Sulbactam or Clindamycin.

front: What pneumonia pathogen is classic in chronic alcoholics with bulging fissure sign?
back:
• Klebsiella pneumoniae: Encapsulated Gram-negative rod causing upper lobe consolidation with bulging
interlobar fissure.

front: What specialized agar is used to culture Legionella pneumophila?
back:
• BCYE Agar: Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract agar (requires iron and L-cysteine).
🐀 Heat Disorders

front: How are Heat Exhaustion and Heat Stroke differentiated clinically?
back:
• Heat Exhaustion: Core temp < 40°C (104°F), sweating intact, NORMAL mental status.
• Heat Stroke: Core temp >= 40°C (104°F), altered mental status (confusion, coma, seizures), anhidrosis
(dry hot skin).

front: What are the two types of Heat Stroke?
back:
• Classic (Non-Exertional): Elderly/immobile individuals during heat waves.


• Exertional: Young athletes or military recruits exercising in hot humid conditions.

front: What is the immediate primary life-saving treatment for Heat Stroke?
back:
• Rapid Cooling: Evaporative/convective cooling or ice water immersion to lower core temp < 39°C within
30 minutes.

front: Why are antipyretics (Aspirin/Paracetamol) contraindicated in Heat Stroke?
back:
• Contraindication: Antipyretics act on hypothalamic fever set point (ineffective in hyperthermia) and
worsen hepatic/renal impairment and bleeding.

front: What organ damage complications occur in severe Heat Stroke?
back:
• Complications: Rhabdomyolysis, Acute Kidney Injury (myoglobinuria), Disseminated Intravascular
Coagulation (DIC), Hepatic necrosis.

front: What is Heat Cramps and its treatment?
back:
• Definition: Painful involuntary muscle spasms during heavy exercise due to hyponatremia/electrolyte
loss.
• Treatment: Rest in cool environment + oral electrolyte/saline replacement.


🐀 Fungal Infections

front: What is the opportunistic fungus that causes Cryptococcal Meningitis in AIDS patients?
back:
• Organism: Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated budding yeast).
• Transmission: Inhalation of pigeon droppings/soil.
• CD4 Threshold: Occurs when CD4 < 100 cells/μL.

front: What CSF diagnostic tests confirm Cryptococcus neoformans?
back:
• India Ink Stain: Shows characteristic halo around clear encapsulated yeast cells.
• Cryptococcal Antigen (CrAg): Highly sensitive ELISA / lateral flow assay in CSF and serum.
• Mucicarmine Stain: Stains thick polysaccharide capsule bright red.

front: What is the induction, consolidation, and maintenance treatment for Cryptococcal Meningitis?
back:
• Induction (2 weeks): IV Amphotericin B + Oral Flucytosine.
• Consolidation (8 weeks): High-dose oral Fluconazole (400 mg daily).
• Maintenance: Oral Fluconazole (200 mg daily) until CD4 > 100 for >= 3 months.

front: What is the microscopic morphology of Aspergillus fumigatus?
back:
• Morphology: Septate hyphae with acute angle branching (45 degrees).
• Fungus Ball: Aspergilloma forming in pre-existing TB cavities.

front: How do you distinguish Aspergilloma vs Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA) vs Invasive Aspergillosis?
back:
• Aspergilloma: Non-invasive fungal ball in old cavity; presents with hemoptysis.
• ABPA: Hypersensitivity reaction in asthma/CF patients; elevated IgE and eosinophilia.
• Invasive Aspergillosis: Angioinvasive in neutropenic patients; severe triad of fever, pleuritic
chest pain, hemoptysis; CT halo sign.

front: What is the drug of choice for Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: IV / Oral Voriconazole.
• Alternative: Isavuconazole or Liposomal Amphotericin B.

front: What microscopic feature distinguishes Mucorales (Rhizopus / Mucor) from Aspergillus?
back:
• Mucorales: Broad, non-septate (coenocytic) hyphae branching at right angles (90 degrees).
• Aspergillus: Narrow, septate hyphae branching at acute angles (45 degrees).

front: What clinical syndrome is characteristic of Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis?
back:
• Patient Population: Uncontrolled Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) or profound neutropenia.
• Hallmark Signs: Facial pain, orbital proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, black necrotic nasal eschar.
• Pathology: Rapid angioinvasion causing tissue necrosis and cribriform plate extension.

front: What is the emergency management for Rhinocerebral Mucormycosis?
back:
• Medical: High-dose IV Liposomal Amphotericin B.
• Surgical: Immediate radical surgical debridement of necrotic tissue.
• Metabolic: Reversal of diabetic ketoacidosis.

front: What microscopic forms are produced by Candida albicans?
back: • Dimorphic: Forms pseudohyphae and budding yeast at 20°C, and true germ tubes at 37°C.

front: How does Pseudomembranous Candidiasis (Oral Thrush) present?
back:
• Appearance: Creamy white curd-like plaques on oral mucosa.
• Distinguishing Feature: Scrapes off easily leaving a raw, red, bleeding base.

front: What class of antifungals is first-line treatment for Invasive Candidemia in unstable patients?
back:
• Echinocandins: Caspofungin, Micafungin, or Anidulafungin (inhibit cell wall beta-1,3-D-glucan
synthesis).

front: What organism causes Pneumocystis Jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP)?
back:
• Organism: Pneumocystis jirovecii (atypical fungus).
• CD4 Threshold: Occurs when CD4 < 200 cells/μL in HIV.
• Presentation: Exertional dyspnea, non-productive cough, fever, hypoxia out of proportion to
exam.

front: What chest X-ray finding and stain confirm Pneumocystis Jirovecii Pneumonia?
back:
• Chest X-Ray: Bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates ('bat-wing' pattern).
• Stain: Gomori Methenamine Silver (GMS) stain showing crushed ping-pong ball cysts in
BAL/sputum.

front: What is the drug of choice for PCP treatment and prophylaxis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: High-dose Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX / Cotrimoxazole).
• Adjunctive Corticosteroids: Indicated if PaO2 < 70 mmHg or A-a gradient >= 35 mmHg.

front: What dimorphic fungus is associated with bird/bat droppings in caves and river valleys?
back:
• Histoplasma capsulatum: Intracellular yeast inside macrophages; causes granulomatous lung
lesions.

front: What dimorphic fungus is known as 'Desert Rheumatism' or 'Valley Fever'?
back:
• Coccidioides immitis: Endemic in Southwest USA/desert soil; forms spherules filled with
endospores in tissue.

front: What dimorphic fungus presents with broad-based budding yeast?
back:
• Blastomyces dermatitidis: Broad-based budding yeast; causes pulmonary and granulomatous
skin lesions.
🐀 COVID-19

front: What is the causative agent and cellular receptor for COVID-19?
back:
• Causative Agent: SARS-CoV-2 (enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus).
• Cellular Receptor: ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2) receptor on type II pneumocytes.

front: What is the classic HRCT chest imaging hallmark of COVID-19 pneumonia?
back:
• HRCT Findings: Bilateral, peripheral, subpleural Ground-Glass Opacities (GGOs) with crazy-paving
pattern.

front: What laboratory markers reflect hyperinflammation and poor prognosis in severe COVID- 19?
back:
• Cytokine Storm Markers: Lymphopenia, elevated Ferritin, high D-dimer, elevated CRP, LDH, and


IL-6.

front: What transmission-based precautions are required for SARS-CoV-2 during aerosol- generating procedures?
back:
• Precautions: Airborne precautions — Negative-pressure isolation room + N95/FFP3 respirator
mask + face shield.

front: What severe secondary fungal infection rose dramatically during COVID-19 treatment?
back:
• COVID-19-Associated Mucormycosis (CAM): Seen in diabetic patients receiving high-dose
corticosteroids.

front: What antiviral drug is approved for early outpatient or hospitalized COVID-19 patients?
back:
• Paxlovid (Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir): Oral protease inhibitor (for early non-hospitalized high-risk
cases).
• Remdesivir: IV RNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor.

front: What immunosuppressive therapy reduces 28-day mortality in hospitalized severe COVID- 19 requiring oxygen?
back:
• Dexamethasone: 6 mg daily for 10 days (RECOVERY trial).
• IL-6 Inhibitor: Tocilizumab (added in severe hyperinflammatory disease).

front: What thrombotic complication is common in severe COVID-19?
back:
• Prothrombotic State: High incidence of Pulmonary Embolism (PE) and Deep Vein Thrombosis
(DVT); prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is standard.

front: What is MIS-C (Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children)?
back:
• Definition: Rare post-viral hyperinflammatory syndrome occurring 2-6 weeks after COVID-19 in
children.
• Features: High fever, Kawasaki-like signs (conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash), coronary
aneurysms, shock.

front: What is the primary diagnostic gold standard test for active COVID-19?
back: • Nasopharyngeal RT-PCR: Detects SARS-CoV-2 viral RNA.

front: How long is the typical incubation period for SARS-CoV-2?
back: • Incubation Period: 2 to 14 days (average 4-5 days).

front: What gastrointestinal manifestations occur in COVID-19?
back:
• Symptoms: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea (ACE2 expressed in
enterocytes).

front: What neurological symptoms are early sensory indicators of COVID-19?
back: • Anosmia (loss of smell) and Dysgeusia (taste distortion).

front: What defines 'Post-COVID-19 Condition' (Long COVID)?
back:
• Definition: Symptoms persisting > 12 weeks after initial infection (fatigue, brain fog, shortness of
breath) not explained by alternative diagnoses.
🐀 HIV

front: What family and genus does HIV belong to, and what enzymes does it carry?
back:
• Family: Retroviridae (Lentivirus genus).
• Enzymes: Reverse Transcriptase, Integrase, Protease.
• Structural Glycoproteins: gp120 (attachment to CD4) and gp41 (fusion).

front: What primary cellular receptors and co-receptors does HIV bind to?
back:
• Primary Receptor: CD4 molecule on T-helper lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells.
• Co-Receptors: CCR5 (macrophage-tropic) and CXCR4 (T-cell-tropic).

front: What genetic mutation confers resistance to HIV-1 infection?
back:
• CCR5-delta 32 Mutation: Homozygous deletion prevents HIV gp120 binding and entry into host
cells.

front: What is the CDC definition of AIDS?
back:
• Criteria: Absolute CD4 count < 200 cells/μL OR CD4 percentage < 14% OR presence of an AIDS-


defining opportunistic condition.

front: What is Acute Retroviral Syndrome (ARS)?
back:
• Timing: 2 to 4 weeks post-exposure.
• Presentation: Mononucleosis-like illness (fever, painful lymphadenopathy, maculopapular rash,
sore throat, myalgias).
• Serology: High viral load, p24 antigen positive, antibodies negative (window period).

front: What is the recommended screening and confirmatory testing algorithm for HIV?
back:
• Screening: 4th Generation HIV-1/2 Antigen/Antibody Combination Immunoassay (detects p24
antigen + anti-HIV antibodies).
• Confirmation: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay or HIV-1 RNA PCR.

front: What opportunistic infection occurs when CD4 < 200 cells/μL and its prophylaxis?
back:
• Infection: Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia (PCP).
• Prophylaxis: Daily single-strength or double-strength TMP-SMX.

front: What opportunistic infection occurs when CD4 < 100 cells/μL and its prophylaxis?
back:
• Infections: Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis, Cryptococcal meningitis.
• Prophylaxis: Daily double-strength TMP-SMX (covers both PCP and Toxoplasma).

front: What opportunistic infection occurs when CD4 < 50 cells/μL and its prophylaxis?
back:
• Infections: Mycobacterium avium Complex (MAC), Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis.
• Prophylaxis: Weekly Azithromycin (for MAC).

front: How does CNS Toxoplasmosis present on brain CT/MRI in HIV?
back:
• Presentation: Focal neurological deficits, seizures, headaches.
• MRI Finding: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in basal ganglia.

front: How is Primary CNS Lymphoma differentiated from Toxoplasmosis on MRI?
back: • Primary CNS Lymphoma: Usually SINGLE ring-enhancing lesion, EBV-DNA positive in CSF.

front: What pathognomonic funduscopic finding indicates CMV Retinitis in AIDS?
back: • Funduscopy: 'Pizza-pie' appearance (retinal hemorrhage + yellow fluffy white infiltrates).

front: What malignancy is caused by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) in AIDS?
back:
• Kaposi Sarcoma: Violaceous/purple macules, nodules, or plaques on skin, oral mucosa, and
visceral organs.

front: What pathogen causes Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) in AIDS?
back:
• Pathogen: JC Virus (Polyomavirus).
• MRI Finding: Demyelination without mass effect or ring enhancement in subcortical white matter.

front: What is the standard antiretroviral therapy (ART) backbone for treatment-naive HIV patients?
back:
• Regimen: 2 NRTIs + 1 INSTI (Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitor).
• Example: Biktarvy (Bictegravir + Emtricitabine + Tenofovir alafenamide).

front: What fatal adverse effect is associated with Abacavir and how is it prevented?
back:
• Toxicity: Severe hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, GI distress, dyspnea).
• Prevention: Screen for HLA-B*5701 allele prior to initiating Abacavir.

front: What NRTI causes renal toxicity and decreased bone mineral density?
back:
• Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF): Causes Fanconi syndrome (proximal renal tubular
acidosis) and osteomalacia.

front: What NNERTI drug is famous for causing vivid dreams and CNS side effects?
back: • Efavirenz: Causes vivid dreams, insomnia, psychosis, and teratogenicity (neural tube defects).

front: What is Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS)?
back:
• Definition: Paradoxical clinical worsening of treated or latent opportunistic infection shortly after
starting ART due to rapid CD4 recovery.

front: What is Occupational Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV?
back:
• Timing: Start within 2 hours (must be within 72 hours of exposure).
• Duration: 28 days of 3-drug ART (Emtricitabine + Tenofovir + Raltegravir/Dolutegravir).

front: What is Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV?
back:
• Definition: Daily oral Truvada (TDF/FTC) or Descovy (TAF/FTC) taken by uninfected high-risk
individuals.

front: What fungal pathogen causes chronic diarrhea in AIDS when CD4 < 100?
back:
• Cryptosporidium parvum: Acid-fast oocysts in stool causing severe watery non-bloody diarrhea.
🐀 Malaria

front: What species of Plasmodium cause human Malaria and which is most lethal?
back:
• Species: Plasmodium falciparum (most lethal), P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi.
• Lethality: P. falciparum causes microvascular sequestration, cerebral malaria, and severe anemia.

front: What is the vector and transmission route of Malaria?
back:
• Vector: Female Anopheles mosquito (bites between dusk and dawn).
• Infective Stage: Sporozoites injected into human bloodstream during blood meal.

front: What Plasmodium stage infects human hepatocytes and erythrocytes?
back:
• Hepatocytes (Exo-erythrocytic stage): Sporozoites enter liver cells and become Schizonts.
• Erythrocytes (Erythrocytic stage): Merozoites released from liver invade RBCs.

front: Which Plasmodium species produce dormant hypnozoites in the liver causing relapses?
back:
• Hypnozoite Species: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale.
• Treatment: Primaquine or TAFENOQUINE required to eradicate liver hypnozoites.

front: What key laboratory test MUST be performed before administering Primaquine?
back:
• Test: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency screen.
• Risk: Primaquine causes severe intravascular hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

front: What are the fever paroxysm intervals for different Plasmodium species?
back:
• Tertian Fever (Every 48 hours): P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale.
• Quartan Fever (Every 72 hours): Plasmodium malariae.
• Quotidian Fever (Every 24 hours): Plasmodium knowlesi.

front: What erythrocyte inclusions are characteristic of P. vivax vs P. falciparum?
back:
• P. vivax / P. ovale: Schüffner's dots (fine pink stippling).
• P. falciparum: Maurer's clefts / double ring forms / banana-shaped gametocytes.

front: What thin/thick blood film findings confirm P. falciparum Malaria?
back:
• Thick Smear: Highly sensitive for detecting presence of parasites.
• Thin Smear: Gold standard for species identification and calculating parasite percentage.
• P. falciparum Morphologies: Multiple delicate ring forms per RBC, banana/crescent-shaped
gametocytes.

front: What is Cerebral Malaria?
back:
• Pathophysiology: P. falciparum PfEMP-1 protein causes infected RBC cytoadherence to brain
capillaries.
• Presentation: Encephalopathy, coma, seizures, retinal hemorrhages.

front: What is Blackwater Fever?
back:
• Definition: Severe intravascular hemolysis caused by P. falciparum or quinine therapy.
• Manifestation: Hemoglobinuria (dark red/black urine) and acute renal failure.

front: What is the first-line treatment for Uncomplicated P. falciparum Malaria?
back:
• Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (ACT): Coartem (Artemether + Lumefantrine) or
Dihydroartemisinin + Piperaquine.

front: What is the first-line treatment for Severe P. falciparum Malaria?
back: • First-Line Drug: IV / IM Artesunate for at least 24 hours, followed by a full oral ACT course.

front: What genetic traits confer natural resistance against Malaria?
back:
• Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS): Protects against severe P. falciparum.
• Duffy Antigen Negative (Fy a-b-): Protects against P. vivax invasion.
• Thalassemia & G6PD Deficiency.

front: What chemoprophylaxis regimens are used for travelers to chloroquine-resistant malaria areas?
back:
• Atovaquone-Proguanil (Malarone): Daily; start 1-2 days before, during, and 7 days post-travel.
• Doxycycline: Daily; start 1-2 days before, during, and 4 weeks post-travel.
• Mefloquine: Weekly; approved in pregnancy.

front: What rapid diagnostic test (RDT) targets P. falciparum antigen?
back: • PfHRP2 (Histidine-Rich Protein 2): Detects P. falciparum in blood.

front: What causes Tropical Splenomegaly Syndrome (Hyperreactive Malarial Splenomegaly)?
back:
• Pathophysiology: Chronic immune hyperresponsiveness to malarial antigen causing massive
splenomegaly, elevated IgM, and hepatic sinusoidal lymphocytosis.
🐀 Tuberculosis

front: What is the causative agent and staining property of Tuberculosis?
back:
• Organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
• Cell Wall: Rich in Mycolic Acids (lipid-dense).
• Stain: Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) — positive on Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain (bright red rods on blue
background).

front: What is a Ghon Focus, Ghon Complex, and Ranke Complex?
back:
• Ghon Focus: Primary subpleural lung parenchymal lesion (middle/lower lobe).
• Ghon Complex: Ghon focus + ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
• Ranke Complex: Calcified Ghon complex (healed primary TB).

front: Where does Secondary (Reactivation) Pulmonary TB characteristically localize?
back: • Anatomic Location: Apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes (high oxygen tension).

front: What is the hallmark histological lesion of Tuberculosis?
back:
• Histology: Caseating (cheese-like) granulomas surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans
multinucleated giant cells, and lymphocytes.

front: What are the classic constitutional symptoms of Pulmonary TB?
back:
• Symptoms: Chronic cough (> 2-3 weeks), hemoptysis, low-grade evening fever, drenching night
sweats, anorexia, weight loss.

front: How is the Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux test) performed and interpreted?
back:
• Technique: Intradermal injection of 5 TU PPD; read induration diameter at 48-72 hours.
• >= 5 mm Positive: HIV, recent TB contact, organ transplant, immunosuppressed.
• >= 10 mm Positive: Healthcare workers, immigrants from endemic zones, diabetics, IV drug
users.
• >= 15 mm Positive: Healthy individuals with no risk factors.

front: What advantage does Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) have over Mantoux test?
back:
• IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB): Measures IFN-gamma released by T-cells exposed to ESAT-6/CFP-10
antigens.
• Advantage: NOT affected by prior BCG vaccination; requires single blood visit.

front: What culture media are used to grow Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
back:
• Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) Medium: Egg-based solid medium; slow growth (3 to 6 weeks).
• MGIT (Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube): Liquid culture system (faster, 1-2 weeks).

front: What rapid molecular test detects M. tuberculosis and Rifampicin resistance simultaneously?
back: • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: Automated real-time PCR providing results within 2 hours.

front: What is the standard RIPE first-line anti-TB treatment regimen and duration?
back:
• Intensive Phase (2 months): Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol.
• Continuation Phase (4 months): Rifampicin + Isoniazid.
• Total Duration: 6 months.

front: What key side effect and mandatory supplement are associated with Isoniazid (INH)?
back:
• Side Effects: Peripheral neuropathy (due to Pyridoxine deficiency) and Hepatotoxicity.
• Mandatory Co-prescription: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine 10-50 mg daily).

front: What side effects are associated with Rifampicin?
back:
• Side Effects: Orange-red discoloration of body fluids (tears, urine, sweat), potent Cytochrome
P450 inducer, hepatotoxicity.

front: What side effect is pathognomonic for Ethambutol?
back:
• Toxicity: Retrobulbar Optic Neuritis (red-green color blindness and decreased visual acuity).
• Monitoring: Baseline and monthly visual acuity/color vision testing.

front: What side effect is classic for Pyrazinamide?
back: • Toxicity: Hyperuricemia (gouty arthritis) and hepatotoxicity.

front: What defines Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB) and Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR- TB)?
back:
• MDR-TB: Resistant to at least BOTH Isoniazid and Rifampicin.
• XDR-TB: Resistant to INH, Rifampicin + ANY Fluoroquinolone + at least one 2nd-line injectable
(Amikacin/Kanamycin/Capreomycin) or Bedaquiline/Linezolid.

front: What novel drugs are used to treat MDR-TB?
back: • New Oral Agents: Bedaquiline (ATP synthase inhibitor) and Pretomanid / Delamanid.

front: What is Pott's Disease?
back:
• Definition: Tuberculous spondylitis (TB of the spine).
• Location: Lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae.
• Complications: Anterior vertebral collapse, kyphosis (gibbus deformity), cold psoas abscess.

front: What is Scrofular lymphadenitis?
back: • Definition: TB lymphadenitis of cervical lymph nodes ('king's evil'); painless cold enlargement.

front: What is Miliary Tuberculosis?
back:
• Pathophysiology: Hematogenous dissemination of TB bacilli throughout the body.
• Chest X-Ray: 1-2 mm uniform 'millet seed' nodular infiltrates throughout both lungs.

front: Why are corticosteroids added to anti-TB therapy in Tuberculous Meningitis or Pericarditis?
back: • Indication: Reduces mortality, cerebral edema, and constrictive pericarditis.

front: What isolation room setup is mandatory for hospitalized pulmonary TB patients?
back:
• Airborne Isolation: Negative-Pressure isolation room with >= 12 air changes per hour +
healthcare workers wear N95 respirators.

front: What is Latent TB Infection (LTBI) treatment?
back:
• LTBI Definition: Positive TST/IGRA, NO symptoms, NORMAL chest X-ray.
• Regimens: 9 months of INH daily OR 3 months of weekly INH + Rifapentine.

front: What BCG vaccine type is used and its primary protection?
back:
• Vaccine: Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis strain.
• Protection: Prevents severe disseminated TB and TB meningitis in young infants.

front: What pleural fluid finding indicates Tuberculous Pleurisy?
back:
• Pleural Fluid Analysis: Exudative, lymphocyte-predominant, high Adenosine Deaminase (ADA >
40 U/L).
🐀 Leptospirosis

front: What is the causative agent and morphology of Leptospirosis?
back:
• Organism: Leptospira interrogans (thin, motile, tightly coiled spirochete with hooked ends like a
question mark).

front: What is the main animal reservoir and transmission route of Leptospirosis?
back:
• Reservoir: Rodents (rats excreted in urine).
• Transmission: Exposure of abraded skin/mucous membranes to water, soil, or mud contaminated
with infected rat urine (sewer workers, farmers, kayakers).

front: What biphasic clinical course characterizes Leptospirosis?
back:
• Anteric (Leptospiremic) Phase (Days 1-7): Sudden high fever, severe calf muscle tenderness,
conjunctival suffusion.
• Immune Phase (Days 10+): IgM antibody appearance, meningitis, renal/hepatic dysfunction.

front: What physical exam sign is pathognomonic for Leptospirosis?
back: • Conjunctival Suffusion: Bilateral redness of scleral conjunctiva WITHOUT purulent discharge.

front: What severe life-threatening syndrome is known as Weil's Disease?
back:
• Weil's Disease Triad: Jaundice + Acute Kidney Injury + Hemorrhagic diathesis (pulmonary


hemorrhage).

front: What reference serological test is the gold standard for Leptospirosis diagnosis?
back:
• Microscopic Agglutination Test (MAT): Uses live leptospira antigens to detect specific
agglutinating antibodies.

front: In which specimens can Leptospires be isolated during Week 1 vs Week 2?
back:
• Week 1: Isolated from Blood and CSF.
• Week 2 onwards: Isolated from Urine.

front: What is the treatment of choice for Mild vs Severe Leptospirosis?
back:
• Mild Outpatient: Oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID) for 7 days.
• Severe (Weil's Disease): IV Penicillin G (1.5 MU IV q6h) or IV Ceftriaxone.

front: What reaction may occur within hours of starting Penicillin for Leptospirosis?
back:
• Jarisch-Herxheimer Reaction: Sudden fever, chills, hypotension due to massive spirochete lysis
and endotoxin release.

front: What kidney lesion is produced by Leptospira interrogans?
back: • Pathology: Acute Interstitial Nephritis and acute tubular necrosis (non-oliguric hypokalemic AKI).

front: What oral antibiotic is used for short-term prophylaxis in high-risk Leptospira exposures?
back: • Prophylaxis: Oral Doxycycline (200 mg weekly).

front: How is dark-field microscopy used in Leptospirosis?
back:
• Dark-Field Microscopy: Direct visualization of motile spirochetes with hooked ends in fresh
blood or urine.
🐀 H. Pylori

front: What is the microbiology and colonization site of Helicobacter pylori?
back:
• Microbiology: Gram-negative microaerophilic spiral/curved bacillus with polar flagella.
• Site: Deep mucosal gel layer of the gastric antrum.

front: What enzyme produced by H. pylori neutralizes stomach acid?
back:
• Urease Enzyme: Cleaves urea into ammonia (NH3) and CO2; ammonia neutralizes gastric acid
creating an alkaline microenvironment.

front: What major gastrointestinal diseases are linked to chronic H. pylori infection?
back:
• Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD): 90% duodenal ulcers, 70% gastric ulcers.
• Gastric Cancer: Gastric Adenocarcinoma and MALT Lymphoma.

front: What non-invasive test is gold standard for diagnosing active H. pylori and confirming eradication?
back:
• Urea Breath Test (UBT): Patient ingests 13C/14C labeled urea; labeled CO2 measured in exhaled
breath.
• Stool Antigen Test: Excellent alternative for active infection.

front: Why is serology (IgG) useless for confirming H. pylori eradication?
back:
• Limitation: Anti-H. pylori IgG antibodies remain positive in blood for months/years even after
successful cure.

front: What medications MUST be discontinued prior to Urea Breath Test or Stool Antigen Test?
back:
• PPIs (Proton Pump Inhibitors): Discontinue for at least 2 weeks.
• Antibiotics & Bismuth: Discontinue for at least 4 weeks.

front: What is the standard Bismuth-Based Quadruple Eradication Regimen?
back: • Quadruple Therapy (14 days): PPI + Bismuth Subsalicylate + Metronidazole + Tetracycline.

front: What is standard Clarithromycin-Based Triple Eradication Regimen?
back:
• Triple Therapy (14 days): PPI + Clarithromycin + Amoxicillin (or Metronidazole). *Used only
where clarithromycin resistance < 15%.

front: What happens to low-grade Gastric MALT Lymphoma after H. pylori eradication?
back:
• Regression: Complete tumor regression occurs in > 75% of low-grade MALT cases solely after
antibiotic eradication of H. pylori.

front: What Rapid Urease (CLO) endoscopic biopsy test color change indicates positive H. pylori?
back:
• CLO Test: Biopsy placed in urea medium with phenol red; urease generates ammonia raising pH
\rightarrow turns from Yellow to Bright Pink.
🐀 Fever & FUO

front: What is the classic Petersdorf and Beeson definition of Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO)?
back:
• Criteria: Fever >= 38.3°C (101°F) on several occasions, lasting for >= 3 weeks, without a diagnosis
after 1 week of inpatient investigation (or 3 outpatient visits).

front: What are the four major diagnostic categories of FUO?
back:
• Infections (30-40%): TB, endocarditis, intra-abdominal abscesses, brucellosis.


• Malignancies (20-30%): Lymphomas (Hodgkin/Non-Hodgkin), Renal cell carcinoma, Leukemia.
• Connective Tissue / Autoimmune (15-20%): Still's disease, Temporal Arteritis, SLE.
• Miscellaneous: Drug fever, thyroiditis, pulmonary embolism.

front: What classic fever patterns correspond to specific infectious diseases?
back:
• Pel-Ebstein Fever: Alternating high fever for days followed by afebrile period (Hodgkin
Lymphoma).
• Undulant Fever: Wave-like rise and fall (Brucellosis).
• Step-Ladder Fever: Gradual stepwise rise each evening (Typhoid fever).
• Quotidian/Tertian/Quartan: Daily/48h/72h spikes (Malaria).

front: What disease presents with high quotidian fever, salmon-pink evanescent rash, and arthritis?
back:
• Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD): Classic cause of FUO with markedly elevated serum Ferritin
(> 5 times normal).

front: What is Drug Fever?
back:
• Definition: Adverse reaction to drugs (Beta-lactams, Sulfonamides, Phenytoin) occurring 7-10


days after starting; resolves within 48-72 hours of drug discontinuation.

front: What nuclear imaging modality is useful in localized FUO workup?
back:
• PET-CT (FDG-PET/CT): Highly sensitive for identifying occult inflammatory foci, vascular lesions
(large vessel vasculitis), and occult lymphomas.

front: What is Classic Nosocomial (Hospital-Acquired) FUO?
back:
• Definition: Fever >= 38.3°C in hospitalized patient receiving acute care, with no fever on
admission, and negative evaluation after 3 days (causes: C. diff, catheter sepsis, DVT, drug fever).

front: What is Neutropenic FUO?
back:
• Definition: Fever >= 38.3°C with Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) < 500 cells/μL; requires
immediate empiric antipseudomonal IV coverage (Cephepime/Pip-Tazo).

front: What disease causes temporal headache, jaw claudication, high ESR, and FUO in elderly?
back:
• Temporal (Giant Cell) Arteritis: Requires immediate high-dose Steroids to prevent irreversible
blindness.
🐀 UTI

front: What is the most common pathogen causing uncomplicated Community-Acquired Urinary Tract Infection?
back: • Escherichia coli (Uropathogenic E. coli): Responsible for 80-85% of uncomplicated UTIs.

front: What pathogen is a common cause of uncomplicated UTI in sexually active young females?
back:
• Staphylococcus saprophyticus: Coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant Gram-positive
staphylococcus (10-15% of cases).

front: What bacterial pathogen produces urease leading to staghorn calculus formation?
back:
• Proteus mirabilis: Urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia, raising urine pH (> 8) and precipitating
struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) stones.

front: How is Acute Cystitis differentiated from Acute Pyelonephritis clinically?
back:
• Acute Cystitis: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain. NO systemic signs.
• Acute Pyelonephritis: Fever, chills, flank pain, Costovertebral Angle (CVA) tenderness, nausea,
vomiting, WBC casts.

front: What urinalysis findings indicate bacterial UTI?
back:
• Leukocyte Esterase: Indicates pyuria (presence of WBCs).
• Nitrite Test: Indicates presence of Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) that reduce
nitrates to nitrites.

front: What microscopic urinalysis finding is pathognomonic for Acute Pyelonephritis?
back: • WBC Casts: Indicates renal parenchymal infection/inflammation.

front: What colony count defines significant bacteriuria on midstream clean-catch urine culture?
back: • Definition: >= 10^5 CFU/mL (Colony Forming Units per mL) of a single organism.

front: What first-line oral antibiotics are recommended for acute uncomplicated cystitis?
back:
• Nitrofurantoin: 100 mg BID for 5 days.
• Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX): 1 DS tablet BID for 3 days.
• Fosfomycin: 3g single dose.

front: What first-line outpatient oral therapy is recommended for uncomplicated Pyelonephritis?
back: • Oral Fluoroquinolone: Ciprofloxacin (500 mg BID) or Levofloxacin (750 mg daily) for 7 days.

front: When is Asymptomatic Bacteriuria treated with antibiotics?
back:
• Mandatory Indications: Pregnant women (prevents pyelonephritis and preterm labor) AND
patients undergoing invasive urological procedures.
• Do NOT Treat: Healthy non-pregnant women, elderly, catheterized patients.

front: What defines a Complicated UTI?
back:
• Definition: UTI in presence of structural/functional urinary tract abnormality, catheters, diabetes,
renal failure, immunosuppression, or in MEN.

front: What is Catheter-Associated UTI (CAUTI) prevention strategy?
back:
• Primary Prevention: Avoid unnecessary urinary catheterization; remove catheters as early as
possible.

front: What antibiotic is contraindicated for Pyelonephritis?
back:
• Nitrofurantoin: Does NOT achieve therapeutic tissue levels in renal parenchyma (concentrates
only in bladder).

front: What is Emphysematous Pyelonephritis?
back:
• Definition: Severe necrotizing renal parenchymal infection with gas formation seen in diabetic
patients; caused by E. coli / Klebsiella.
🐀 Septicemia & Septic Shock

front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of Sepsis?
back:
• Definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to
infection.
• Organ Dysfunction Criterion: Increase in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score
by >= 2 points.

front: What criteria constitute the quick SOFA (qSOFA) bedside screening tool?
back:
• 1. Respiratory Rate >= 22 breaths/min.
• 2. Altered Mental Status (GCS < 15).
• 3. Systolic Blood Pressure <= 100 mmHg.
• Score >= 2: Indicates high risk of poor outcomes.

front: What clinical criteria define Septic Shock under Sepsis-3?
back:
• Definition: Subset of sepsis with profound circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities.
• Criteria: Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg AND
serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

front: What are the core components of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign '1-Hour Bundle'?
back:
• 1. Measure blood lactate level.
• 2. Obtain blood cultures prior to starting antibiotics.
• 3. Administer broad-spectrum IV antimicrobials.
• 4. Rapidly infuse 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate >= 4 mmol/L.
• 5. Apply vasopressors if hypotensive during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP >= 65.

front: What is the first-line vasopressor of choice in Septic Shock?
back:
• First-Line Vasopressor: Norepinephrine (potent alpha-1 agonist with modest beta-1 activity).
• Second-Line Agent: Vasopressin (added to reduce norepinephrine dosage).

front: What IV fluid is recommended for initial resuscitation in sepsis?
back:
• Crystalloids: Balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's or Plasmalyte) or 0.9% Normal Saline at 30
mL/kg within 3 hours.

front: What laboratory marker reflects tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism in shock?
back:
• Serum Lactate: Elevated lactate (> 2-4 mmol/L) indicates cellular hypoxia; clearance of lactate


monitors response to resuscitation.

front: What serum biomarker aids in distinguishing bacterial sepsis from viral infection or non- infectious SIRS?
back:
• Procalcitonin (PCT): Rises rapidly in response to systemic bacterial endotoxins; used to guide
antibiotic initiation and de-escalation.

front: What hemodynamic change characterizes early Warm Septic Shock vs late Cold Shock?
back:
• Warm Shock (Hyperdynamic): High Cardiac Output (CO), LOW Systemic Vascular Resistance
(SVR), warm wide pulse pressure extremities.
• Cold Shock (Hypodynamic): Low CO, high SVR, cold clammy extremities.

front: What hematological complication manifests as petechiae, purpura, and bleeding from venipuncture sites in sepsis?
back:
• Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC): Uncontrolled microvascular thrombosis
consuming platelets and coagulation factors (elevated PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer).

front: When are IV corticosteroids (Hydrocortisone) indicated in Septic Shock?
back:
• Indication: Refractory septic shock requiring ongoing vasopressor support despite fluid
resuscitation (Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV).

front: What blood pressure target is maintained during septic shock resuscitation?
back: • Target: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) >= 65 mmHg.

front: What dynamic parameter is preferred over static CVP to assess fluid responsiveness?
back:
• Dynamic Measures: Stroke Volume Variation (SVV), Pulse Pressure Variation (PPV), or Passive
Leg Raise (PLR) test.

front: What is Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome?
back:
• Definition: Fulminant meningococcemia causing massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhagic necrosis,
DIC, and fatal septic shock.

front: What bacterial toxin acts as a Superantigen to trigger Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)?
back:
• TSST-1 (Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1) from Staph aureus OR Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxin A
from Group A Strep.
• Mechanism: Cross-links MHC class II to V-beta region of T-cell receptors, causing massive
polyclonal T-cell activation and cytokine storm.

front: What is the clinical presentation of Staphylococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome?
back:
• Signs: High fever, hypotension, diffuse sunburn-like desquamating erythroderma (palms/soles
desquamate 1-2 weeks later), multi-organ failure (tampon use / surgical wound).
🐀 Filariasis

front: What parasitic nematode is the primary cause of Lymphatic Filariasis (Elephantiasis)?
back: • Pathogen: Wuchereria bancrofti (responsible for 90% of cases), Brugia malayi, Brugia timori.

front: What mosquito vectors transmit Wuchereria bancrofti?
back: • Vectors: Culex mosquitoes (urban areas), Anopheles and Aedes mosquitoes.

front: What periodicity is characteristic of Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae in blood?
back:
• Nocturnal Periodicity: Microfilariae circulate in peripheral blood primarily at night (10 PM to 2
AM).

front: What is the optimal timing for blood collection to diagnose Wuchereria bancrofti?
back: • Blood Collection: Midnight blood smear (thick blood film collected between 10 PM and 2 AM).

front: What chronic physical deformities result from adult Wuchereria bancrofti worms?
back:
• Pathology: Adult worms live in lymphatic vessels causing mechanical obstruction, lymphangitis,
fibrosis.
• Deformities: Lymphedema, massive swelling of legs/scrotum (Elephantiasis), Hydrocele, Chyluria
(milky urine).

front: What drug of choice treats Lymphatic Filariasis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) — kills microfilariae and adult worms.


• Mass Drug Administration (MDA): DEC + Albendazole (or Ivermectin).

front: What intracellular endosymbiont bacterium lives inside filarial worms and can be targeted with antibiotics?
back:
• Bacterium: Wolbachia.
• Targeting Drug: Doxycycline (6-week course clears Wolbachia, sterilizing and killing adult filarial
worms).

front: What filarial worm causes 'River Blindness'?
back:
• Pathogen: Onchocerca volvulus.
• Vector: Simulium blackfly.
• Manifestations: Subcutaneous nodules, pruritic leopard skin, sclerosing keratitis leading to
blindness.

front: What is the drug of choice for Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)?
back:
• Drug of Choice: Ivermectin (DEC is contraindicated because it causes severe ocular Mazzotti
reaction).

front: What filarial parasite is known as the 'African Eye Worm' causing Calabar swellings?
back:
• Pathogen: Loa loa.
• Vector: Chrysops deerfly (mango fly).
• Signs: Transient angioedema (Calabar swellings), migration of adult worm under conjunctiva.
🐀 Toxoplasmosis

front: What is the causative agent and definitive host of Toxoplasma gondii?
back:
• Organism: Toxoplasma gondii (obligate intracellular protozoan).
• Definitive Host: Domestic and wild cats (felines are the only host where sexual reproduction
occurs).

front: What are the primary modes of human Toxoplasmosis infection?
back:
• Ingestion: Tissue cysts in undercooked meat (pork, lamb).
• Oocysts: Ingestion of cat feces-contaminated soil, water, or unwashed vegetables.
• Congenital: Transplacental transmission during primary maternal infection.

front: What clinical syndrome occurs in immunocompetent adults with acute Toxoplasmosis?
back:
• Presentation: Asymptomatic in 80-90%. Can cause mononucleosis-like illness (painless cervical
lymphadenopathy, fever, fatigue).

front: What is the classical triad of Congenital Toxoplasmosis?
back:
• Classic Triad: Chorioretinitis + Hydrocephalus + Intracranial Calcifications (diffuse ring/nodular
calcifications).

front: What is the hallmark neurological presentation of Toxoplasmosis in AIDS patients?
back:
• CD4 Threshold: Occurs when CD4 < 100 cells/μL.
• MRI Brain: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions with surrounding edema in basal ganglia/cortex.
• Clinical Presentation: Seizures, focal neurological deficits, headache.

front: What is the first-line treatment regimen for acute Toxoplasmosis in AIDS or severe disease?
back:
• Regimen: Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine + Folinic Acid (Leucovorin).
• Folinic Acid Role: Prevents pyrimethamine-induced bone marrow suppression (megaloblastic


anemia).

front: What alternative drug is given for Toxoplasmosis in pregnant women before 18 weeks gestation?
back: • First-Line Pregnancy Drug: Spiramycin (concentrates in placenta to prevent fetal transmission).

front: What alternative drug is used if a patient is allergic to Sulfadiazine?
back: • Alternative Regimen: Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Folinic Acid.

front: How is primary maternal Toxoplasmosis infection diagnosed?
back:
• Serology: Positive T. gondii IgM antibody or 4-fold increase in IgG titer; IgG avidity test confirms
recent vs distant infection.

front: What prophylactic medication prevents Toxoplasmosis in HIV patients with CD4 < 100?
back: • Prophylaxis: Daily double-strength Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

front: What eye manifestation occurs in reactivation of congenital Toxoplasmosis?
back:
• Ocular Toxoplasmosis: Focal necrotizing retinochoroiditis with 'headlight in the fog' appearance
on funduscopy.

front: What microscopic forms exist for T. gondii?
back:
• Tachyzoites: Rapidly multiplying crescent-shaped motile invasive form.
• Bradyzoites: Slow-multiplying form enclosed in tissue cysts (muscles, brain).
• Oocysts: Environmentally resistant form shed in cat feces.

front: What is Sabin-Feldman Dye Test?
back: • Serological Reference Test: Measures neutralizing antibodies against live T. gondii tachyzoites.

front: What advice should be given to non-immune pregnant women regarding cat care?
back:
• Prevention: Avoid changing cat litter boxes, eat only well-cooked meat, wash hands/vegetables
thoroughly.
🐀 Leishmaniosis

front: What protozoan parasite causes Leishmaniasis and what is its insect vector?
back:
• Parasite: Leishmania species (obligate intracellular protozoa).
• Vector: Female Phlebotomine Sandfly.

front: What are the two morphological forms of Leishmania?
back:
• Promastigote: Flagellated, motile form found in sandfly vector.
• Amastigote: Non-flagellated intracellular oval form inside human macrophages (LD bodies).

front: What species cause Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar)?
back:
• Visceral Species: Leishmania donovani (Indian subcontinent/Africa) and Leishmania infantum /
chagasi.

front: What is the classic clinical pentad of Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-Azar)?
back:
• 1. Prolonged irregular fever.
• 2. Massive Splenomegaly (huge spleen) and hepatomegaly.
• 3. Pancytopenia (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia).
• 4. Hypergammaglobulinemia (polyclonal IgG elevation).
• 5. Marked emaciation and hyperpigmentation of skin ('black fever').

front: What specimen provides the highest diagnostic yield for Visceral Leishmaniasis?
back:
• Splenic Aspiration / Biopsy: Highest diagnostic yield (> 95% shows LD bodies in macrophages).
• Bone Marrow Aspiration: Safer alternative (80-85% yield).

front: What rapid serological test detects Visceral Leishmaniasis antibodies?
back:
• rK39 Immunochromatographic Strip Test: Highly sensitive and specific for L. donovani
antibodies.

front: What is the drug of choice for Visceral Leishmaniasis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: Liposomal Amphotericin B (high cure rate, single-day or short course).
• Traditional Alternatives: Sodium Stibogluconate (Pentavalent antimonial) or Miltefosine (oral).

front: What species cause Cutaneous Leishmaniasis ('Oriental Sore')?
back:
• Old World: Leishmania tropica, L. major.
• New World: Leishmania mexicana, L. braziliensis.

front: What is the classic skin lesion of Cutaneous Leishmaniasis?
back:
• Lesion: Painless papule that enlarges into a volcano-like ulcer with raised indurated borders and
central crusting on exposed body parts.

front: What severe destructive form is caused by Leishmania braziliensis?
back:
• Mucocutaneous Leishmaniasis (Espundia): Destruction of nasopharyngeal mucous membranes,
nasal septum perforation, and facial disfigurement.

front: What skin condition occurs years after cured Visceral Leishmaniasis?
back:
• Post-Kala-Azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL): Hypopigmented macules, papules, or nodules on
face and body containing amastigotes.

front: What skin hypersensitivity test is used in Leishmaniasis?
What free-living amoeba causes severe keratitis in contact lens wearers?
back:
• Pathogen: Acanthamoeba castellanii.
• Risk Factor: Rinsing contact lenses with tap water or swimming in contaminated water with
contact lenses.

front: What are the clinical signs and diagnostic findings of Acanthamoeba Keratitis?
back:
• Signs: Severe ocular pain out of proportion to exam, ring-shaped corneal infiltrate, photophobia.
• Diagnosis: Corneal scraping stained with Calcofluor white or confocal microscopy showing


double-walled cysts.

front: What topical antiseptics treat Acanthamoeba Keratitis?
back:
• Topical Antiseptics: Chlorhexidine (0.02%) or Polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) + Brolene
eye drops.

front: What parasite causes 'River Blindness' with ocular keratitis?
back:
• Pathogen: Onchocerca volvulus.
• Vector: Simulium blackfly.
• Ocular Pathology: Microfilariae invade eye causing punctate keratitis, sclerosing keratitis,
chorioretinitis, and permanent blindness.

front: What filarial worm is directly visible crawling across the subconjunctiva of the eye?
back:
• Pathogen: Loa loa ('African Eye Worm').
• Vector: Chrysops deerfly.
• Treatment: Surgical extraction of adult worm from subconjunctiva + Diethylcarbamazine (DEC).

front: What ocular lesion is produced by Toxoplasma gondii?
back:
• Focal Necrotizing Retinochoroiditis: Yellow-white retinal lesion with intense vitreous
inflammation ('headlight in the fog').

front: What parasite causes Ocular Larva Migrans (granuloma in retina mimicking retinoblastoma)?
back:
• Pathogen: Toxocara canis / Toxocara cati (dog/cat roundworm).
• Manifestation: Retinal granuloma causing unilateral vision loss and leukocoria (white pupillary
reflex).

front: What is Cysticercosis of the eye?
back:
• Organism: Larval stage (Cysticercus cellulosae) of Taenia solium.
• Ocular Location: Subretinal space or vitreous humor causing retinal detachment.

front: What fly larva causes Ophthalmomyiasis?
back: • Pathogen: Oestrus ovis (sheep botfly larva) invading conjunctival sac.

front: What ocular lesion occurs in congenital Syphilis?
back:
• Interstitial Keratitis: Bilateral ground-glass corneal opacification occurring in late congenital
syphilis.
🐀 Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers

front: What are the major families of viruses causing Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers (VHFs)?
back:
• Flaviviridae: Dengue, Yellow Fever, Kyasanur Forest disease.
• Filoviridae: Ebola virus, Marburg virus.
• Arenaviridae: Lassa fever, Junin, Machupo.
• Bunyaviridae: Rift Valley Fever (RVF), Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF).

front: What vector transmits Dengue Virus?
back: • Vector: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes (day-biting mosquitoes).

front: What are the clinical signs of Classic Dengue Fever ('Breakbone Fever')?
back:
• Symptoms: High fever, retro-orbital headache, severe retro-bulbar eye pain, severe
myalgias/arthralgias ('breakbone pain'), maculopapular rash.

front: What causes severe Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) / Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS)?
back:
• Mechanism: Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE) during secondary infection with a different
Dengue serotype.
• Key Features: Plasma leakage, severe thrombocytopenia (< 100,000), capillary permeability, fluid
accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion), shock.

front: What tourniquet test result indicates increased capillary fragility in Dengue?
back:
• Positive Tourniquet Test: >= 20 petechiae per square inch after inflating BP cuff midway
between SBP and DBP for 5 minutes.

front: What laboratory antigen test confirms acute early Dengue infection (Days 1-5)?
back: • Dengue NS1 Antigen Test: Positive in blood during early febrile phase.

front: What vector transmits Yellow Fever and what organ is classically targeted?
back:
• Vector: Aedes aegypti mosquito.
• Target Organ: Liver (hepatocellular necrosis with Councilman bodies, jaundice, dark black vomit
/ hematemesis).

front: What type of vaccine is the Yellow Fever vaccine (17D)?
back:
• Vaccine: Live attenuated vaccine (single subcutaneous dose provides lifetime immunity;
mandatory for travel to endemic areas).

front: What vector transmits Rift Valley Fever (RVF)?
back:
• Vector & Reservoir: Aedes and Culex mosquitoes; exposure to fluids/blood of infected livestock
(sheep, goats, cattle).
