front: What vector transmits Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever (CCHF)?
back: • Vector: Hyalomma ticks (or contact with infected livestock blood/tissues).

front: What antiviral drug is effective against Lassa Fever and CCHF?
back: • Antiviral: Intravenous Ribavirin.

front: What natural reservoir host harbors Ebola and Marburg Filoviruses?
back: • Reservoir: Fruit bats (Pteropodidae family).

front: How is Ebola virus transmitted person-to-person?
back:
• Transmission: Direct contact with blood, secretions, organs, or bodily fluids of infected
symptomatic individuals or deceased bodies.

front: What isolation precautions are required for suspected Ebola / VHF patients?
back:
• Strict Contact and Airborne Precautions: Full PPE (impermeable gown, double gloves, fluid-
resistant mask/PAPR, boot covers, face shield) + single isolation room.
🐀 Rabies

front: What family and genome structure does Rabies virus belong to?
back:
• Family: Rhabdoviridae (Lyssavirus genus).
• Structure: Bullet-shaped, enveloped single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus.

front: How is Rabies transmitted to humans?
back:
• Transmission: Saliva of infected mammals via bite, scratch, or lick on broken skin/mucous
membranes.
• Primary Animals: Dogs (worldwide), bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes.

front: How does Rabies travel from bite site to the Central Nervous System?
back:
• Pathophysiology: Binds acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction \rightarrow travels
via Retrograde Axonal Transport along peripheral nerves to spinal cord and brain.

front: What pathognomonic histological lesion confirms Rabies in brain tissue?
back:
• Histology: Negri Bodies (eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusion bodies) in cerebellar Purkinje cells


and hippocampal pyramidal neurons.

front: What are the two clinical forms of Rabies?
back:
• Furious Rabies (80%): Agitation, delirium, hydrophobia (pharyngeal spasms when
seeing/swallowing water), aerophobia, hypersalivation.
• Paralytic (Dumb) Rabies (20%): Progressive ascending quadriparesis mimicking Guillain-Barré
syndrome.

front: What is the mortality rate of Rabies once clinical symptoms develop?
back: • Mortality: Virtually 100% fatal once symptoms appear (almost no survivors).

front: What defines Rabies Exposure Categories according to WHO?
back:
• Category I: Touching/feeding animals, licks on intact skin (NO prophylaxis needed).
• Category II: Nibbling exposed skin, minor scratches without bleeding (Vaccine needed).
• Category III: Single/multiple transdermal bites, scratches, licks on broken skin, exposure to bats
(Vaccine + Rabies Immunoglobulin [RIG] needed).

front: What is the immediate first step following any animal bite?
back:
• Wound Cleansing: Thoroughly flush and wash bite wound with soap and water under tap for at
least 15 minutes.

front: What constitutes Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for a non-immunized person with Category III rabies bite?
back:
• 1. Wound Washing (15 min).
• 2. Human Rabies Immune Globulin (HRIG): 20 IU/kg infiltrated around bite wound on Day 0.
• 3. Cell-Culture Rabies Vaccine: 4 doses IM (Days 0, 3, 7, 14).

front: What is the observation period for a domestic dog/cat that bites a human?
back:
• Observation: Observe healthy dog/cat for 10 days. If animal remains healthy for 10 days, rabies
PEP is discontinued.
🐀 Cat Scratch Disease

front: What is the causative agent of Cat Scratch Disease?
back: • Organism: Bartonella henselae (fastidious Gram-negative rod).

front: How is Bartonella henselae transmitted to humans?
back:
• Vector & Reservoir: Fleas transmit among cats; transmitted to humans via scratches, bites, or
saliva contact from kittens.

front: What is the typical clinical presentation of Cat Scratch Disease?
back:
• Primary Lesion: Erythematous papule/pustule at scratch site 3-10 days post-exposure.
• Lymphadenopathy: Subacute regional lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, epitrochlear)
developing 1-3 weeks later.

front: What histology is characteristically seen in Cat Scratch lymph nodes?
back: • Histology: Suppurative necrotizing granulomas with microabscesses.

front: What severe vascular lesions are produced by Bartonella in immunocompromised (AIDS) patients?
back:
• Bacillary Angiomatosis: Red-purple vascular skin lesions mimicking Kaposi sarcoma.
• Peliosis Hepatis: Blood-filled cystic spaces in liver.

front: What ocular manifestation is known as Parinaud Oculoglandular Syndrome?
back:
• Presentation: Unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis + ipsilateral preauricular
lymphadenopathy.

front: What special silver stain visualizes Bartonella henselae in biopsy tissues?
back: • Stain: Warthin-Starry silver stain (demonstrates pleomorphic bacilli).

front: What antibiotic accelerates lymph node resolution in Cat Scratch Disease?
back:
• Treatment: Oral Azithromycin (5-day course) or Doxycycline.
🐀 Plague

front: What is the causative agent and staining morphology of Plague?
back:
• Organism: Yersinia pestis (Gram-negative, facultative intracellular coccobacillus).
• Staining: Bipolar staining ('safety-pin' appearance) on Giemsa or Wayson stain.

front: What is the primary vector and animal reservoir of Yersinia pestis?
back:
• Vector: Oriental rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis).
• Reservoirs: Wild rodents (ground squirrels, prairie dogs, rats).

front: What are the three clinical forms of Plague?
back:
• 1. Bubonic Plague: Most common (80-90%).
• 2. Septicemic Plague: Primary or secondary bloodstream invasion.
• 3. Pneumonic Plague: Highly contagious airborne form.

front: What is a 'Bubo' in Bubonic Plague?
back:
• Definition: Extremely painful, swollen, inflamed regional lymph node (groin, axilla, neck) that may
suppurate.

front: What physical manifestation gave rise to the historical term 'Black Death'?
back:
• Black Death: Acral gangrene (necrosis of fingers, toes, nose) secondary to severe DIC and
endotoxic septicemia.

front: How is Pneumonic Plague transmitted person-to-person?
back:
• Transmission: Respiratory droplets from coughing patients (highly contagious, 100% fatal if
untreated within 24 hours).

front: What is the first-line antibiotic treatment for Yersinia pestis?
back:
• First-Line Antibiotic: Intramuscular / IV Streptomycin or Gentamicin.
• Alternatives: Oral / IV Doxycycline or Ciprofloxacin.

front: What post-exposure prophylaxis is given to close contacts of Pneumonic Plague?
back: • PEP: Oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID) or Ciprofloxacin for 7 days.

front: What virulence factor of Yersinia pestis inhibits phagocytosis?
back: • F1 Capsular Antigen: Protein envelope that prevents phagocytosis by host macrophages.

front: What type of isolation is mandatory for Pneumonic Plague?
back: • Droplet Precautions: Strict isolation until 48 hours of effective antibiotic therapy.

front: What diagnostic specimens are collected for suspected Plague?
back: • Specimens: Bubo aspirate, blood culture, sputum / bronchoalveolar lavage.

front: What rapid antigen test detects Yersinia pestis?
back: • F1 Antigen Dipstick Test: Rapid detection of F1 capsular antigen.

front: What mechanism causes flea blockage in Yersinia pestis transmission?
back:
• Biofilm Formation: Y. pestis produces hemin storage biofilm blocking flea proventriculus
\rightarrow starving flea bites repeatedly and regurgitates bacteria into host.

front: What antibiotic is preferred for Plague during pregnancy?
back: • Pregnancy Regimen: Gentamicin.

front: What is Primary Septicemic Plague?
back:
• Definition: Direct inoculation into bloodstream without prior lymph node bubo formation; rapidly
progresses to septic shock.

front: What animal exposure in Southwest USA causes Plague?
back: • Reserves in USA: Prairie dogs, ground squirrels, and domestic cats infected via flea bites.

front: What diagnostic growth pattern is shown by Yersinia pestis in liquid broth?
back:
• Broth Culture: Stalactite growth pattern (clumps hanging from surface broth).
🐀 Infectious Diarrhea

front: What is the primary differentiation between Secretory (Non-Invasive) vs Invasive (Dysenteric) Diarrhea?
back:
• Secretory (Non-Invasive): Watery, large volume, no fecal leukocytes/blood,
epigastric/periumbilical cramping (Vibrio cholerae, ETEC, Rotavirus).
• Invasive (Dysentery): Small volume, bloody stool with mucus and pus (PMNs), tenesmus, high
fever (Shigella, Campylobacter, EIEC, Salmonella).

front: What is the leading cause of Traveler's Diarrhea worldwide?
back:
• Pathogen: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).
• Toxins: Heat-Labile (LT - increases cAMP) and Heat-Stable (ST - increases cGMP) enterotoxins.

front: What bacterial cause of dysentery requires an extremely low infective dose?
back:
• Shigella dysenteriae: Extremely low infective dose (as few as 10-100 organisms can cause severe
disease).
• Complication: Produces Shiga toxin leading to Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).

front: What bacterial pathogen is the leading bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in developed countries?
back:
• Campylobacter jejuni: Microaerophilic curved Gram-negative rod with 'seagull-wing' appearance.
• Transmission: Undercooked poultry or unpasteurized milk.
• Complication: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) and Reactive Arthritis.

front: What pathogen causes gastroenteritis pseudo-appendicitis (right lower quadrant pain)?
back:
• Yersinia enterocolitica: Causes mesenteric adenitis mimicking acute appendicitis; acquired from
contaminated pork.

front: What strain of E. coli causes Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) and why are antibiotics contraindicated?
back:
• Strain: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) O157:H7 (produces Shiga-like toxin / verotoxin).
• Source: Undercooked ground beef.


• Contraindication: Antibiotics INCREASE Shiga toxin release, escalating HUS risk.

front: What clinical triad defines Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)?
back:
• HUS Triad: Microangiopathic Hemolytic Anemia (schistocytes) + Thrombocytopenia + Acute
Kidney Injury.

front: What pathogen causes pseudomembranous colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotic use?
back:
• Clostridioides difficile (C. diff): Anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive rod.
• Toxins: Toxin A (Enterotoxin) and Toxin B (Cytotoxin).
• Antibiotics Implicated: Clindamycin, Fluoroquinolones, Cephalosporins.

front: What is the first-line oral treatment for Clostridioides difficile colitis?
back:
• First-Line Drug: Oral Fidaxomicin (200 mg BID for 10 days) or Oral Vancomycin (125 mg QID for
10 days).
• Refractory / Recurrent: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT).

front: What protozoan causes flask-shaped intestinal ulcers and bloody dysentery?
back:
• Entamoeba histolytica: Trophozoites ingest RBCs (erythrophagocytosis); form flask-shaped
mucosal ulcers in colon.

front: What is the drug of choice for Amoebic Dysentery?
back:
• Tissue Amoebicide: Metronidazole or Tinidazole for 7-10 days.
• Luminal Amoebicide: Followed by Paromomycin or Diloxanide furoate (clears luminal cysts).

front: What viral cause of acute diarrhea is leading worldwide in infants < 5 years?
back:
• Rotavirus (Reoviridae family): Causes severe dehydrating infantile diarrhea; preventable by oral
live rotavirus vaccine.

front: What virus causes outbreaks of epidemic gastroenteritis on cruise ships and schools?
back: • Norovirus (Caliciviridae family): Leading cause of foodborne outbreak diarrhea in adults.

front: What acid-fast protozoan causes chronic diarrhea in immunocompromised / AIDS patients?
back:
• Cryptosporidium parvum: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain shows red spherical oocysts (4-6 μm) in
stool.
🐀 Food Poisoning

front: What bacterial food poisoning presents with rapid onset nausea/vomiting within 1-6 hours?
back:
• Staphylococcus aureus: Preformed heat-stable enterotoxin in mayonnaise, pastries, cream,
processed meats.

front: What pathogen causes food poisoning associated with reheated fried rice?
back:
• Bacillus cereus (Emetic Form): Preformed heat-stable toxin in reheated fried rice (onset 1-5
hours, vomiting).

front: What causes the diarrheal form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning?
back:
• Bacillus cereus (Diarrheal Form): Heat-labile enterotoxin produced in gut after consuming
contaminated meat/vegetables (onset 8-16 hours, diarrhea).

front: What food poisoning pathogen is associated with improperly canned home foods?
back:
• Clostridium botulinum: Anaerobic spore-forming Gram-positive rod producing potent
neurotoxin in canned goods.

front: What is the intracellular mechanism of Botulinum Toxin?
back:
• Mechanism: Cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking presynaptic release of Acetylcholine at
neuromuscular junction \rightarrow causes descending flaccid paralysis.

front: What are the classic clinical features of Foodborne Botulism?
back:
• Symmetrical Descending Flaccid Paralysis: 4 Ds — Diplopia, Dysphagia, Dysarthria, Dyspnea,
dry mouth, fixed dilated pupils.

front: What causes Infant Botulism ('Floppy Baby Syndrome') and its classic risk food?
back:
• Risk Food: Raw Honey containing Clostridium botulinum spores.
• Pathophysiology: Spores germinate in immature infant gut colonizing intestine and releasing
toxin.

front: What treatment is indicated for adult Botulism vs Infant Botulism?
back:
• Adult Foodborne: Equine Trivalent Botulinum Antitoxin.
• Infant Botulism: Human Botulism Immune Globulin (BabyBIG).

front: What food poisoning pathogen causes severe watery diarrhea 8-24 hours after eating warmed meat/poultry dishes?
back:
• Clostridium perfringens (Type A): Spores survive cooking, germinate during slow cooling,
produce enterotoxin in intestine.

front: What pathogen causes foodborne septicemia and meningitis from unpasteurized soft cheese or cold cut meats?
back: • Listeria monocytogenes: Can grow at refrigeration temperatures.

front: What toxin causes Scombroid Fish Poisoning and its clinical presentation?
back:
• Toxin: Histamine toxicity from bacterial breakdown of histidine in inadequately refrigerated dark-


meat fish (tuna, mahi-mahi, mackerel).
• Presentation: Rapid onset facial flushing, peppery taste, throbbing headache, urticaria, wheezing
(treat with antihistamines).

front: What toxin causes Ciguatera Fish Poisoning?
back:
• Toxin: Ciguatoxin from dinoflagellates bioaccumulated in large reef fish (barracuda, grouper).
• Hallmark Sign: Temperature reversal (hot feels cold, cold feels hot) + paresthesias.

front: What food poisoning organism is associated with raw oysters and shellfish in warm coastal waters?
back:
• Vibrio vulnificus & Vibrio parahaemolyticus: Causes severe wound infections, bullous lesions,
and fulminant septicemia in patients with chronic liver disease.

front: What food poisoning agent causes illness within 24-48 hours after eating undercooked eggs or poultry?
back:
• Non-Typhoidal Salmonella (S. enteritidis / S. typhimurium): Causes acute gastroenteritis.
🐀 Cholera

front: What is the causative agent and morphology of Cholera?
back:
• Organism: Vibrio cholerae (O1 and O139 serogroups).
• Morphology: Gram-negative curved/comma-shaped rod with a single polar flagellum ('darting'
motility).

front: How is Vibrio cholerae transmitted?
back: • Transmission: Ingestion of water or food contaminated with human feces (fecal-oral route).

front: What is the intracellular mechanism of action of Cholera Enterotoxin (Choleragen)?
back:
• Mechanism: B-subunit binds GM1 ganglioside; A-subunit ADP-ribosylates Gs protein \rightarrow
permanently activates Adenylate Cyclase \rightarrow massive increase in intracellular cAMP
\rightarrow active secretion of Cl- and Na+ with water into gut lumen.

front: What is the hallmark stool presentation of severe Cholera?
back:
• Stool: Sudden onset painless, profuse watery diarrhea classic for 'Rice-Water Stool' (clear fluid
with flecks of mucus, non-bloody, sweet fishy odor).

front: What major metabolic and fluid volume complications result from untreated Cholera?
back:
• Complications: Severe hypovolemic shock (loss of up to 1 L stool/hour), metabolic acidosis (loss
of HCO3-), hypokalemia.

front: What selective culture medium is used to isolate Vibrio cholerae?
back:
• Medium: TCBS Agar (Thiosulfate-Citrate-Bile Salts-Sucrose agar) — yields large sucrose-
fermenting yellow colonies.

front: What is the absolute cornerstone of Cholera treatment?
back:
• Rehydration Therapy: Immediate fluid restoration.
• Mild/Moderate: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) solution containing glucose, sodium, potassium,
citrate.
• Severe Shock: Rapid IV Ringer's Lactate (up to 100 mL/kg within 3 hours).

front: What antibiotic adjunctive therapy is used in severe Cholera?
back:
• Adjunctive Antibiotic: Single-dose Doxycycline (300 mg PO) or Azithromycin (1g PO in pregnant
women/children).
• Benefit: Shortens disease duration and reduces stool volume output.

front: What oral vaccines are available for Cholera prevention?
back: • Oral Cholera Vaccines (OCVs): Dukoral, Shanchol, Euvichol (killed whole-cell vaccines).

front: Why does gastric acid play a critical protective role against Cholera?
back:
• Acid Lability: Vibrio cholerae is extremely acid-labile; high gastric stomach acid kills most
ingested bacteria (infective dose decreases drastically in patients taking PPIs).
🐀 Anti-Viral Drugs

front: What is the mechanism of action of Acyclovir?
back:
• Mechanism: Guanosine analogue monophosphorylated by viral Thymidine Kinase \rightarrow
triphosphorylated by host enzymes \rightarrow competitively inhibits viral DNA Polymerase
causing chain termination.
• Spectrum: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV.

front: What is the drug of choice for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis / pneumonitis?
back:
• Drug of Choice: Ganciclovir (IV) or Valganciclovir (oral).
• Mechanism: Phosphorylated by CMV UL97 kinase; inhibits viral DNA polymerase.
• Toxicity: Bone marrow suppression (neutropenia).

front: What alternative drug treats Ganciclovir-resistant CMV or Acyclovir-resistant HSV?
back:
• Alternative: Foscarnet (or Cidofovir).
• Mechanism: Direct pyrophosphate analogue; does NOT require viral kinase phosphorylation.
• Toxicity: Severe nephrotoxicity and electrolyte wasting (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia).

front: What is the mechanism of action of Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and Zanamivir?
back:
• Mechanism: Neuraminidase Inhibitors.
• Function: Prevents release of newly formed Influenza A and B viral progeny from infected cell
surface.
• Timing: Must be initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset.

front: Why is Zanamivir contraindicated in asthma patients?
back:
• Contraindication: Zanamivir is an inhaled powder; causes severe bronchospasm in patients with
reactive airway disease (asthma/COPD).

front: What novel single-dose oral drug treats Influenza by inhibiting cap-dependent endonuclease?
back: • Baloxavir Marboxil: Single-dose oral cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor.

front: What are the key classes of Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs) for Hepatitis C?
back:
• NS3/4A Protease Inhibitors: Glecaprevir, Voxilaprevir (-previr).
• NS5A Replication Complex Inhibitors: Velpatasvir, Ledipasvir, Pibrentasvir (-asvir).
• NS5B Polymerase Inhibitors: Sofosbuvir (-buvir).

front: What is the mechanism of action of Ribavirin and its primary toxicity?
back:
• Mechanism: Guanosine analogue; inhibits IMP dehydrogenase and viral RNA polymerase.
• Toxicity: Dose-dependent Hemolytic Anemia and severe Teratogenicity (contraindicated in
pregnancy).

front: What mechanism of action defines NRTIs (Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors)?
back:
• Mechanism: Competitive inhibition of HIV reverse transcriptase causing DNA chain termination
(e.g., Tenofovir, Emtricitabine, Abacavir, Lamivudine, Zidovudine).

front: What mechanism of action defines NNRTIs?
back:
• Mechanism: Non-competitive allosteric binding to HIV reverse transcriptase enzyme (e.g.,
Efavirenz, Rilpivirine, Nevirapine).

front: What mechanism of action defines HIV Protease Inhibitors?
back:
• Mechanism: Inhibits HIV aspartyl protease, preventing cleavage of Gag-Pol polyproteins,
producing immature non-infectious virions (e.g., Darunavir, Atazanavir, Ritonavir).

front: What mechanism of action defines INSTIs (Integrase Inhibitors)?
back:
• Mechanism: Blocks integration of HIV viral DNA into host chromosome (e.g., Bictegravir,
Dolutegravir, Raltegravir).

front: What HIV entry inhibitor binds CCR5 co-receptor?
back: • Maraviroc: Selective CCR5 antagonist (requires tropism assay before use).

front: What HIV fusion inhibitor binds viral gp41?
back:
• Enfuvirtide (T-20): Subcutaneous injection blocking gp41 conformational change.
🐀 Zoonotic Diseases

front: What animal reservoir and vector transmit Lyme Disease?
back:
• Organism: Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete).
• Vector: Ixodes scapularis blacklegged tick.
• Reservoir: White-footed mouse (larvae/nymphs) and white-tailed deer (adult ticks).

front: What pathognomonic skin rash defines Stage 1 Lyme Disease?
back: • Erythema Migrans: Expanding 'bull's-eye' rash with central clearing at tick bite site.

front: What treatment is indicated for early Lyme Disease?
back:
• First-Line Drug: Oral Doxycycline (100 mg BID) for 14-21 days.
• Pregnancy / Children < 8 yrs: Oral Amoxicillin or Cefuroxime.

front: What organism causes Q Fever and how is it acquired?
back:
• Organism: Coxiella burnetii (obligate intracellular bacterium).
• Transmission: Inhalation of aerosols from amniotic fluid/placenta of infected sheep, goats, or
cattle during birthing.
• Presentation: Culture-negative endocarditis, atypical pneumonia, hepatitis.

front: What organism causes Anthrax and its classic microscopic morphology?
back:
• Organism: Bacillus anthracis (large Gram-positive spore-forming rod in boxcar chains with poly-
D-glutamic acid capsule).

front: What skin lesion is classic for Cutaneous Anthrax?
back: • Lesion: Painless black necrotic eschar surrounded by extensive gelatinous edema.

front: What is Inhalation Anthrax ('Woolsorter's Disease') radiological hallmark?
back: • Radiology: Mediastinal widening on chest X-ray due to hemorrhagic mediastinitis.

front: What organism causes Tularemia ('Rabbit Fever')?
back:
• Organism: Francisella tularensis (Gram-negative coccobacillus).
• Transmission: Direct contact with infected rabbits, tick/deerfly bites, handling animal carcasses.

front: What organism causes Orf Nodule?
back:
• Organism: Parapoxvirus (Orf virus).
• Exposure: Direct contact with infected sheep or goats; causes a solitary hemorrhagic nodule on
hands of butchers/shepherds.

front: What organism causes Erysipeloid in fishermen and butchers?
back:
• Organism: Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae (Gram-positive rod).
• Manifestation: Sharply demarcated violaceous/purplish cellulitis of fingers/hands without
suppuration.
🐀 Levels of Prevention & Immunization

front: What defines Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Prevention in Infectious Diseases?
back:
• Primary Prevention: Preventing disease BEFORE it occurs (vaccination, water sanitation,
mosquito nets).
• Secondary Prevention: Early detection and prompt treatment to interrupt progression
(screening tests like Pap smear, Mantoux test, HIV screening).
• Tertiary Prevention: Reducing disability and rehabilitation from established disease
(physiotherapy post-stroke/polio, chronic disease management).

front: What vaccines are Live Attenuated vs Inactivated / Killed?
back:
• Live Attenuated: MMR, Varicella, Yellow Fever, BCG, Oral Polio (Sabin), Oral Typhoid (Ty21a),
Rotavirus, Intranasal Influenza.
• Killed / Inactivated: Inactivated Polio (Salk), Rabies, Hepatitis A, Whole-cell Cholera, Injectable
Influenza.

front: Why are Live Attenuated Vaccines contraindicated in severely immunocompromised patients and pregnant women?
back:
• Contraindication: Attenuated live viral/bacterial strains can revert or replicate uncontrolled,
causing severe disseminated vaccine-derived infection.

front: What compulsory vaccines are administered to infants at birth in Egypt?
back:
• Birth Vaccines: BCG (intradermal left shoulder), Hepatitis B (IM right thigh), Oral Polio (Zero
dose).

front: What is the Pentavalent compulsory child vaccine composition?
back:
• Pentavalent Vaccine: Diphtheria + Tetanus + Pertussis (DTaP) + Hepatitis B + Haemophilus
influenzae type b (Hib).
• Schedule: Given at 2, 4, and 6 months of age.

front: What is the MMR vaccine administration schedule and route?
back:
• MMR: Measles, Mumps, Rubella.
• Doses: 1st dose at 12 months, 2nd dose at 18 months (Subcutaneous injection).

front: What vaccines are recommended for travelers to Sub-Saharan Africa?
back:
• Mandatory: Yellow Fever vaccine (17D).
• Recommended: Meningococcal MenACWY vaccine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid, Rabies, Malaria
chemoprophylaxis.

front: What vaccine is mandatory for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims to Saudi Arabia?
back:
• Mandatory Vaccine: Quadrivalent Meningococcal Vaccine (MenACWY) administered >= 10 days
prior to arrival.

front: What defines Herd Immunity?
back:
• Definition: Resistance of a population to the spread of an infectious disease when a sufficient
proportion of individuals are immune (threshold typically 80-95%).

front: What is Passive vs Active Immunization?
back:
• Active Immunization: Administration of antigens (vaccines) to stimulate host immune system to
produce long-lasting antibodies.


• Passive Immunization: Administration of preformed antibodies (immunoglobulins) for
immediate temporary protection.

front: What tetanus prophylaxis is given for a dirty wound in an unimmunized person?
back:
• Unimmunized / Unknown (< 3 doses): Tetanus Toxoid Vaccine (Tdap/Td) PLUS Tetanus
Immune Globulin (TIG 250 units IM).

front: What tetanus prophylaxis is given for a clean wound in a fully vaccinated person (> 10 yrs ago)?
back:
• Clean Wound (> 10 yrs since last booster): Tetanus Toxoid Vaccine booster ONLY (No TIG
needed).
🐀 Post Exposure Prophylaxis

front: What is the single most important immediate action following an occupational needle stick injury?
back:
• Immediate Action: Wash needle stick wound thoroughly with soap and running water for several
minutes (Do NOT squeeze or suck wound).

front: What is the average risk of bloodborne virus transmission percutaneous injury?
back:
• Hepatitis B (HBeAg+): ~30% (300 per 1000).
• Hepatitis C: ~3% (30 per 1000).
• HIV: ~0.3% (3 per 1000).

front: What is the optimal window to initiate HIV PEP following exposure?
back:
• Timing: Ideally within 2 hours, MUST be initiated within 72 hours of exposure.
• Duration: 28 days of 3-drug antiretroviral regimen.

front: What Hepatitis B PEP is given to a non-vaccinated healthcare worker exposed to HBsAg+ blood?
back:
• Non-Vaccinated Worker: 1 dose HBIG (Hepatitis B Immune Globulin) + Complete 3-dose HepB
vaccine series initiated within 24 hours.

front: What Hepatitis B PEP is given to a vaccinated worker with anti-HBs >= 10 mIU/mL?
back: • Known Responder (anti-HBs >= 10): NO PEP or vaccine booster required (fully protected).

front: Is PEP recommended for occupational Hepatitis C exposure?
back:
• No Antiviral PEP for HCV: Immunoglobulins and antivirals are NOT recommended for post-
exposure prophylaxis.
• Protocol: Baseline testing for Anti-HCV and HCV RNA, with follow-up testing at 3-6 months; treat
with DAAs if active HCV infection develops.

front: What PEP is indicated for Rabies Category III animal bite in a non-immunized individual?
back:
• PEP Regimen: Human Rabies Immune Globulin (HRIG 20 IU/kg infiltrated at wound) + 4-dose
Rabies Cell-Culture Vaccine (Days 0, 3, 7, 14).

front: What PEP is indicated for close contacts of Meningococcal Meningitis?
back:
• Chemoprophylaxis: Oral Rifampicin (600 mg BID for 2 days) OR single dose Ciprofloxacin (500
mg PO) OR Ceftriaxone (250 mg IM).

front: What PEP is indicated for Varicella-Zoster exposure in non-immune pregnant women?
back:
• PEP: Varicella-Zoster Immune Globulin (VZIG) administered within 96 hours (up to 10 days) of


exposure.

front: What PEP is indicated for Pertussis exposure in close household contacts?
back:
• Chemoprophylaxis: Oral Azithromycin (5 days) or Clarithromycin for all household contacts
regardless of vaccination status.
🐀 Community & Nosocomial Infections

front: What defines a Nosocomial (Healthcare-Associated) Infection?
back:
• Definition: Infection acquired in a hospital or healthcare facility that was neither present nor
incubating at the time of admission (typically developing >= 48 hours after admission).

front: What are the four most common types of Healthcare-Associated Infections (HAIs)?
back:
• 1. Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI) — most common.
• 2. Surgical Site Infections (SSI).
• 3. Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections (CLABSI).
• 4. Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) — highest mortality.

front: What ESKAPE pathogens are major causes of multidrug-resistant nosocomial infections?
back:
• E: Enterococcus faecium (VRE).
• S: Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
• K: Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL / Carbapenemase).
• A: Acinetobacter baumannii.
• P: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
• E: Enterobacter species.

front: What resistance mechanism defines Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)?
back:
• Mechanism: mecA gene encodes altered Penicillin-Binding Protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for
beta-lactam antibiotics.
• Drug of Choice: IV Vancomycin, Daptomycin, or Linezolid.

front: What antibiotic class treats Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus (VRE)?
back: • First-Line Agents: Linezolid or Daptomycin.

front: What defining pigment and odor are produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
back:
• Pigments: Pyocyanin (blue-green) and Pyoverdine (fluorescent yellow-green).
• Odor: Sweet grape-like or fruity odor.

front: What antipseudomonal beta-lactam antibiotics treat Pseudomonas infections?
back:
• Penicillins: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo).
• Cephalosporins: Ceftazidime, Cefepime.
• Carbapenems: Meropenem, Imipenem.
• Monobactam: Aztreonam.

front: What key bundle measures prevent Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infections (CLABSI)?
back:
• CLABSI Bundle: Maximal sterile barrier precautions during insertion, chlorhexidine skin
antisepsis, avoidance of femoral vein, daily assessment of line necessity.

front: What key bundle measures prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP)?
back:
• VAP Bundle: Elevate head of bed 30-45 degrees, daily sedation vacation and extubation readiness


trial, subglottic secretion suctioning, oral care with chlorhexidine.

front: What defines Extended-Spectrum Beta-Lactamase (ESBL) producing bacteria?
back:
• Definition: Enzymes (in E. coli, Klebsiella) that hydrolyze penicillins, cephalosporins, and
aztreonam.
• Drug of Choice: Carbapenems (Meropenem / Imipenem).

front: What is the primary mode of transmission of hospital-acquired pathogens between patients?
back:
• Transmission: Transiently contaminated hands of healthcare workers (Hand Hygiene is the single
most effective preventive measure).

front: What hospital pathogen causes severe pseudomembranous colitis post-antibiotics?
back:
• Clostridioides difficile: Spores survive alcohol hand rubs; requires soap and water handwashing.
🐀 Infection Prevention & Control

front: What are the WHO '5 Moments for Hand Hygiene'?
back:
• 1. Before touching a patient.
• 2. Before clean/aseptic procedures.
• 3. After body fluid exposure risk.
• 4. After touching a patient.
• 5. After touching patient surroundings.

front: When is Soap and Water mandatory over Alcohol-Based Hand Rub?
back:
• Mandatory Soap & Water: When hands are visibly soiled with dirt/blood/fluids AND after caring
for patients with spore-forming pathogens (Clostridioides difficile, Anthrax).

front: What constitute Standard Precautions in infection control?
back:
• Standard Precautions: Applied to ALL patients regardless of diagnosis — hand hygiene, PPE
based on exposure risk, safe injection practices, environmental cleaning, respiratory hygiene.

front: What three types of Transmission-Based Precautions exist?
back:
• 1. Contact Precautions: Gown + Gloves (MRSA, VRE, C. diff, Scabies).


• 2. Droplet Precautions: Surgical mask within 3 feet (N. meningitidis, Influenza, Pertussis,
Mumps).
• 3. Airborne Precautions: N95 respirator + Negative-pressure isolation room (TB, Measles,
Varicella, COVID-19 aerosol procedures).

front: What parameters define proper Steam Autoclave Sterilization?
back:
• Autoclave Parameters: Saturated steam under pressure at 121°C (250°F) for 15-20 minutes at 15
psi pressure (kills all vegetative bacteria, viruses, and bacterial spores).

front: What biological indicator is used to monitor Autoclave efficacy?
back: • Biological Indicator: Spores of Geobacillus stearothermophilus.

front: What color-coded waste bags correspond to medical waste types?
back:
• Yellow Bag: Infectious waste, anatomical waste, soiled dressings, anatomical tissue.
• Red Bag: Contaminated recyclable plastic waste (catheters, IV tubing, syringes without needles).
• Black / Brown Bag: General non-infectious municipal waste.
• Yellow Puncture-Proof Sharps Container: Needles, scalpels, lancets, glass slides.

front: What is High-Level Disinfection (HLD) vs Sterilization?
back:
• Sterilization: Complete destruction of ALL microbial life including bacterial spores (Autoclave,
Ethylene oxide).
• HLD: Kills all microorganisms EXCEPT large numbers of bacterial spores (Glutaraldehyde 2%,
Peracetic acid; used for endoscopes).

front: What Spaulding classification defines Critical, Semi-Critical, and Non-Critical medical items?
back:
• Critical Items: Enters sterile tissue/vascular system (surgical instruments) \rightarrow Requires
STERILIZATION.
• Semi-Critical Items: Contacts intact mucous membranes (endoscopes, anesthesia tubes)
\rightarrow Requires HIGH-LEVEL DISINFECTION.
• Non-Critical Items: Contacts intact skin (stethoscopes, BP cuffs) \rightarrow Requires
LOW/INTERMEDIATE DISINFECTION.

front: What environmental disinfectant is effective against C. diff spores and blood spills?
back:
• Disinfectant: Sodium Hypochlorite (Household Bleach 1:10 dilution).
🐀 Cutaneous Manifestations

front: What skin rash is characteristic of Typhoid Fever vs Meningococcemia?
back:
• Typhoid Fever: Rose Spots (transient, pink, blanching macules on trunk).
• Meningococcemia: Non-blanching petechial and purpuric rash progressing to purpura fulminans.

front: What dermatological sign defines Ecthyma Gangrenosum?
back:
• Definition: Painless indurated erythematous papule that rapidly evolves into a necrotic black
eschar with surrounding erythema.
• Pathogen: Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia.

front: What skin rash defines Erythema Migrans in Lyme Disease?
back: • Erythema Migrans: Expanding 'bull's-eye' rash with central clearing.

front: What dermatological signs define Secondary Syphilis?
back:
• Secondary Syphilis: Maculopapular rash involving PALMS and SOLES + Condylomata Lata (moist
painless warty lesions in anogenital area).

front: What skin rash defines Scarlet Fever?
back:
• Scarlet Fever: Diffuse coarse 'sandpaper-like' erythematous rash + Pastia's lines in skin creases +
Strawberry tongue (Group A Streptococcus).

front: What skin lesion defines Erythema Nodosum and its common infectious causes?
back:
• Erythema Nodosum: Painful, tender, red/violaceous subcutaneous nodules on anterior shins.
• Infectious Causes: Streptococcal pharyngitis, Primary TB, Histoplasmosis, Coccidioidomycosis,
Sarcoidosis.

front: What skin lesions define Infective Endocarditis?
back:
• Janeway Lesions: Painless erythematous macules on palms and soles (septic microemboli).
• Osler Nodes: Painful tender nodular lesions on pads of fingers and toes (immune complex
deposition).
• Splinter Hemorrhages: Linear dark red streaks under fingernails.

front: What cutaneous lesion defines Orf Nodule vs Erysipeloid?
back:
• Orf Nodule: Solitary hemorrhagic umbilicated nodule on hand from sheep contact (Parapoxvirus).
• Erysipeloid: Violaceous non-suppurative cellulitis with raised border on hands of
fishermen/butchers (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae).

front: What skin lesion defines Cutaneous Anthrax?
back:
• Painless black necrotic eschar with extensive non-pitting edema.
🐀 Parasitology

front: What nematode causes Löffler's syndrome (eosinophilic pneumonitis during lung larval migration)?
back:
• Pathogen: Ascaris lumbricoides (also Hookworms - Necator/Ancylostoma and Strongyloides).
• Symptoms: Transient dry cough, wheezing, eosinophilia, migratory pulmonary infiltrates; stool
microscopy for eggs is negative during lung phase.

front: What parasite causes severe nocturnal perianal pruritus in young children?
back:
• Pathogen: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm).
• Diagnosis: Cellophane (Scotch) tape test applied to perianal skin first thing in morning.

front: What nematode is associated with heavy infestation causing Rectal Prolapse in children?
back:
• Pathogen: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).
• Egg Morphology: Barrel/lemon-shaped eggs with prominent bipolar plugs.

front: What hookworms cause microcytic hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia?
back:
• Pathogens: Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.
• Pathophysiology: Adult worms attach to intestinal mucosa and suck blood (0.2 mL
blood/worm/day).

front: What nematode completes its entire life cycle inside human host causing Hyperinfection Syndrome?
back:
• Pathogen: Strongyloides stercoralis.
• Auto-infection: Filariform larvae penetrate perianal skin (larva currens rash).
• Hyperinfection: Massive systemic larval migration carrying gut bacteria in corticosteroid-treated
patients causing fatal sepsis.

front: What Schistosoma species causes Urinary Schistosomiasis and bladder squamous cell carcinoma?
back:
• Pathogen: Schistosoma haematobium.
• Egg Morphology: Oval egg with a distinct TERMINAL spine.
• Complications: Terminal hematuria, dysuria, bladder calcification, Squamous Cell Carcinoma of
bladder.

front: What Schistosoma species cause Intestinal Schistosomiasis and portal hypertension?
back:
• Schistosoma mansoni: Egg with a prominent LATERAL spine.
• Schistosoma japonicum: Small rounded egg with a tiny lateral knob/spine.
• Pathology: Granulomatous response to eggs trapped in liver presinusoidal portal venules
\rightarrow Symmers' pipestem periportal fibrosis and portal hypertension.

front: What tapeworm is acquired from eating undercooked pork and causes Neurocysticercosis?
back:
• Pathogen: Taenia solium (pork tapeworm).
• Neurocysticercosis: Ingestion of T. solium EGGS (not undercooked meat) leads to larval cysticerci
in brain causing adult-onset seizures.

front: What tapeworm is acquired from eating undercooked beef vs freshwater fish?
back:
• Beef Tapeworm: Taenia saginata (unarmed scolex without hooks; causes mild GI symptoms).
• Fish Tapeworm: Diphyllobothrium latum (largest human tapeworm; competes for Vitamin B12
causing Megaloblastic Anemia).

front: What is the single drug of choice for treating all Schistosomiasis and most Trematode/Cestode infections?
back:
• Drug of Choice: Praziquantel (increases cell membrane permeability to calcium, causing muscular
paralysis and detachment of worms).
